maintopic: ARTS, LETTERS AND SCIENCES ANNOUNCEMENT OF SCHOLARSHIP AWARDS TO INDIAN STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will be interested to learn that for the 1961-62 school year, 26 scholarships ranging in value from $250 to $1,750 are being awarded to Indian students of outstanding ability to encourage them to continue with their studies. The greatest number of scholarships previously given in any year since the government instituted this program in 1957 was 18, so the 26 awards for this year represent a substantial and encouraging increase.
Indians from Ontario and Quebec shared 14 scholarships; six were awarded in Saskatchewan and three each in the maritimes and British Columbia. The new awards include eight for university training; three for teacher training; four for nursing; six for various kinds of vocational training; four for studies in the arts; and, for the first time, one for forestry. It is particularly interesting to note the wide range of studies chosen by the recipients of university scholarships, which include dentistry, medicine, law, engineering and home economics.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether statements made during the last two days at Accra in Ghana by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce behind closed doors, we are told, but given to the press in whole or in part, were approved in advance by the government.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have not been able to secure a copy of those statements as yet, though I have endeavoured to do so. Communication between Canada and Accra by telephone is a major difficulty. I tried to do so yesterday afternoon for a number of hours. However, I think I should say at this time that throughout the years this party has stood for a strong commonwealth, and this during the days when there were others in other parts of the house who did not hold that view.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS
speechtext: Including South Africa.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS
speechtext:
We still believe in the maintenance of a strong and effective commonwealth. That we have succeeded in many of the things we have endeavoured to do in that connection is apparent from the fact that we brought about a trade and economic conference. If anyone has any doubt about the stand we have taken in that regard he has but to read Taylor's book on the commonwealth, "The Years of Challenge".
Whatever the statements made may have been, any discussion thereon will be fruitless until those statements are available. The view of this government was expressed by me yesterday and on previous occasions. Our desire is not in any way to interfere with the right of any other member of the commonwealth to determine the course it will take, any more than other parts of the commonwealth can determine ours. However, we have the right among ourselves to point out the potential or possible effects of the action of any member of the commonwealth on the other members. Our desire is a strong and effective commonwealth, and to that end are our purposes directed and our representations made.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of what the Prime Minister has said, and before I ask a supplementary question, may I be permitted to say that not only do we on this side agree that there should be a strong commonwealth, but we believe that if it

had not been for Liberal government policy in Canada in the past there might not have been any commonwealth at all.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS
speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he would consider it proper if the United Kingdom government indulged in the same kind of public criticism of Canadian policy that Canadian ministers are now aiming publicly at United Kingdom government policy on a matter so politically controversial as the one we are talking about.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to answer that question. When the hon. gentleman protests as to the attitude taken by this government to the commonwealth I would just recall the fact that in 1956 his leader said the days of power, in so far as the United Kingdom and France were concerned, were over. That was their attitude to Britain.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS
speechtext: That is not what he said. On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, when the Prime Minister sees fit to quote in this house from one of his predecessors, he should quote accurately and not misrepresent what was said.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister. The Minister of Finance said at Accra, as reported by the Southam news service:
The United Kingdom cannot have a foot in each group and retain the freedom of action which is necessary to the leadership of the commonwealth.
Was he speaking for the government, or expressing the views of the government at that time?

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have
already made very clear the views of the government with respect to this matter. I am not going to discuss reported statements until I see the remarks that have actually been made. 1 have seen reports of statements allegedly made by both the hon. gentleman and the Leader of the Opposition that I am sure they did not make. I am giving the same consideration to some of the remarks allegedly made at this conference.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS
speechtext: In view of the fact that the Prime Minister has mentioned me, may I say that when I am faced with a quotation of that kind, which he says I did not make, I do not give it to the press in advance.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS
speechtext:
I seem to recall one which had to do with-no; that was a statement on a television program.
Inquiries of the Ministry

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS
speechtext:
I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister based upon an excerpt from a speech made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on this same occasion at Accra. The excerpt is as follows:
And so we in Canada are convinced that we are considering not only an economic problem which has far reaching implications for all of us, but also a problem which involves the future of the commonwealth itself. We strongly urge the government of the U.K. to consider this matter in this broader concept when the negotiations with the E.C.M. countries commence in the near future, and ensure that the trading arrangements which exist between the U.K. and her commonwealth partners which have been mutually beneficial over so many years remain unchanged.
My question is this. Is it the view of the government that any effort by any member of the commonwealth to change its trading pattern places the commonwealth itself in jeopardy?

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS
speechtext:
That is another of those hypothetical questions based on a hypothetical quotation. I think it is perfectly clear that each member of the commonwealth may take the course it desires at all times, giving the fullest consideration, as Mr. Macmillan said would be the fact, to the effect it would have on other members of the commonwealth.
Indeed, I rely very strongly on the statement which the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom made in the House of Commons that an application was made for membership to the end that through negotiation the situation might be determined. He also stated -and I know this is the attitude of the United Kingdom government, and at all times it has been their attitude during the period in which the responsibility of government has rested upon my colleagues and myself-that in anything they do every consideration is given by them to assuring the achievement of that which is the common objective of both our governments, namely a strong and effective commonwealth, and that nothing should be done without the fullest consideration and regard always being paid to the welfare of all other members.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister a question arising out of what he has just said. In view of what he has said, will the right hon. gentleman instruct the ministers concerned to stop their public squealing before Canada is hurt?

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS
speechtext:
I do not think the hon. gentleman is very much concerned about the latter part. I think that was an addition to the question. I have seen statements made by the hon. gentleman to which I might

Inquiries of the Ministry have ascribed the same words that he now ascribes to the statement which has been read.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS
speechtext: I wonder if I may direct a supplementary question to the Prime Minister. Are we to understand from the answers he has given with respect to the statements which appear in quotation marks, alleged to have been made by the ministers in Accra, that there was no agreed position which the ministers were to take, determined in advance in Ottawa?

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS
speechtext: The agreed position was declared by me on behalf of this party and the government, in the house.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS
speechtext: Evidently the ministers did not understand it.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CURRENT SITUATION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CURRENT SITUATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I apologize for not sending him notice owing to the rush of affairs. My question is this. In view of the recent disturbing developments which have taken place in the Congo, is the Secretary of State for External Affairs in a position to comment on the present situation in Katanga province?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CURRENT SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I share the concern which I know is felt by all hon. members of this house at the turn of events in Katanga. I am disturbed by the most recent press reports as to the apparent deterioration in the situation there. As I told the house on Wednesday last, it had been our hope that the action taken by the United Nations forces in the Congo would forestall the outbreak of large scale violence and would bring the potentially dangerous situation there effectively under control.
In view of the absence as yet of direct reports from our own people in the Congo, or of an official report from the United Nations command on the most recent developments, I do not wish to go any further than this in offering detailed comment at this stage. As the house is aware the secretary general, Mr. Hammarskjold, is still in Leopoldville, and will be in a position to report personally on these developments when he returns to New York in the near future.

Mr. Chairman, yesterday in a discussion of air force matters the hon. member for Trinity put on the record some fantastic figures of his own devising as to the cost of the acquisition of the F-101 airplane and the manning of the Pine Tree line that were involved in this particular deal. At the time I said if the allegation had come from a serious source I would have taken it seriously. However, I considered the source from which it came and merely said the figures the hon. gentleman was producing were comparable to figures he had produced before, which were quite evidently out. The Canadian Press carried a story in one of the morning newspapers making use of those figures and I think, therefore, I should refer back to what I said in connection with the cost to Canada of the acquisition of the F-101 and the manning of the radar stations on the Pine Tree line.
In order that there may be no question as to what the cost is, I refer to the figures I gave on June 13, which are the estimate of responsible officials of the department. They are the figures which will be used so far as the coming year's operations are concerned in the estimates which are put before this house for approval. I think they are the accurate figures and the figures that must be accepted.

At that time, on June 13, I said in answer to a question by the hon. member for Laurier that the annual cost of civilian staff operation and maintenance-this is the cost for the radar stations of the Pine Tree line which Canada has agreed to take over-is estimated at $5 million for 1961-62; $9.6 million for 1962-63; $15.1 million for 1963-64 and $16.1 million when the stations are fully manned. The NORAD agreement is to run until 1968, when it will be reviewed. The total estimated cost during that period is $94.1 million.
Then there was a supplementary question as to the cost of armed services personnel. I said that the military personnel, of course, will be provided from within existing R.C.A.F. staffs. The total number which will be required to man these stations will be in the neighbourhood of 1,700 to 1,800-I am speaking from memory now but I know it is in that area-and some 800 to 900 civilian staff. There was a further supplementary question, and I said that the estimated cost of the 1,700 to 1,800 military personnel which will be involved in manning these stations when the take-over is complete is around $9 million a year.
I should like to point out that I stated the plan was to provide these out of existing members of the R.C.A.F. The estimate of the total cost of manning the Pine Tree line and the cost for the support for the F-101, which we have to pay for, is $170 million rather than the $490.9 million which the hon. member represented was going to be the cost. In this case, I think he had it for ten years. However, that is the actual figure, $170 million.
This estimate is made up of the cost of the civilian staff and maintenance, which I have mentioned, of $94.1 million; $14.1 million for the spares and support that we have to secure for the F-101; $61.8 million for the cost of military personnel. In addition, of course, under the deal we are giving $50 million of mutual aid and the United States is giving approximately $150 million in the form of F-104 airplanes to our NATO allies in Europe. This $200 million is to be spent in Canada for the production of F-104 airplanes. This is, of course, one of the very attractive features of this whole deal, and will provide $200 million worth of business which means a very large amount of employment to Canadian workers.
Those are the costs and the definite costs. In view of the completely irresponsible calculations which the hon. member for Trinity made and which, unfortunately, have been printed, I thought I should make this definite statement so there would be no question as to what the costs are in connection with this whole deal.
At the same time the hon. member for Trinity talked about the costs of the F-101

and the manning of the Pine Tree line, he referred also to evidence given by the present chairman of the chiefs of staff committee, the then deputy minister, before the defence expenditures committee as to the cost of the Arrow. He made an allegation that the statement of the present chiefs of staff committee was contrary to the figures which I had given relating to what would have been the cost of the Arrow. He subsequently accused me of lying and, of course, was completely out of order so he had to retract; nevertheless that appeared in the newspapers.
I should like to make it clear that the figures I have given in connection with this matter at various times were figures which I quoted from the proceedings of the special committee on defence expenditures. I had in my hand a copy of those minutes and read from them when I gave the figures. The whole story is here in these minutes of the special committee on defence expenditures; therefore there does not need to be any argument as to what the figures are or what was said.
I should like, however, in order to show that the present chairman of the chiefs of staff committee used the same figures which I used, refer to his evidence as found on page 136 of the regular proceedings for Friday, May 12, 1960. He stated at that time:
So the figures to which the minister has referred in the amount of $7.8 million per copy is the average cost of the 100 aeroplanes.
This was on the presumption at that time, or the basis, that 100 airplanes would be secured. I should furthermore like to point out, however, that if the number had been reduced to the number of F-lOl's which we have actually secured, that is to 66, the cost per copy would be considerably higher and as a matter of fact would have come to something in the neighbourhood of $9 million for that smaller number of planes.
However, the main point is this, I think. All statements which I have made in connection with the cost of these planes were taken directly from the figures of the subcommittee and are substantiated by the officials in the department. These various allegations that I have been attempting to mislead the house and to give incorrect figures have no foundation in fact, as I think is quite apparent, I would hope that there would be no more wild statements of that kind.
The matter of continuing to flog the Arrow situation, of course, in view of the fact that it is now some considerable time since the contract was cancelled, I do not think gets us very far, where the discussion of the present estimates of the Department of National Defence is concerned. However, I think these

Last night just before the supper hour the hon. member for Greenwood I thought made a very profound statement, and I think it certainly refers to this area of the R.C.A.F. perhaps even more than to any other area. He said that we on this side appeared to be dealing with unreality or war games, whereas the minister was dealing with reality. When the hon. member for Greenwood says anything we on this side of the chamber listen, and indeed we search ourselves to find out just exactly the reason for what he has said.
I am the first to admit that we are only a part of the whole, or that we are only a small link in this chain. However, it seems to me that we in this committee are concerned with deciding just how effective or how strong this link is, with the dreadful realization that a chain is only as strong as all its links. Why is it that the minister's statements have this air of unreality? I cannot help feeling that we have a defence policy in reverse. What we are doing is this. We decide that we are a small partner with limited resources and that we can do only a very little. We therefore adjust the threat to what we are prepared to meet, in terms of the small area with which we are dealing in our relations with our allies.
Yesterday one or two examples of that tendency arose under the army estimates, when we asked about the Canadian army looking after the shore lines of North America. No matter how often the Minister of National Defence says that the army is concerned with dealing with parachutists and stopping them from taking over our radar installations, I cannot believe that in an all-out nuclear war they would send planes anywhere near the radar installations without realizing that the whole strategic air command would be on them before the parachutists had taken over the D.E.W. line or any other area.
The same criticism applies with respect to the navy estimates. The hon. member for Trinity has suggested that the anti-submarine activities of the Canadian navy are completely and hopelessly out of date in relation to the kind of nuclear submarines that we know the Russians are making. What are we using for our knowledge? The hon. member for Trinity is using a great deal of material from the United States congress. To some extent I have been using material from the London institute of strategic studies, which has attempted to make some study of the threat. They tell us that the Russians have 500 submarines, 10 of which are atomic powered submarines.

I accept that point of order, Mr. Chairman, and will continue. I meant this only as an example of the same thing as that with which we are dealing now. The point is this. The reason for this feeling of unreality in the defence estimates is that what we are doing is adjusting the threat to what we think we can handle in our particular area in conjunction with our allies. I refer to this item for the R.C.A.F. We know that Russia is moving into the missile field. We know that we can do very little in this area, and indeed that the United States can do very little. So once again we adjust the threat to what we think we can deal with.
I tried to find out what the minister thinks the threat is. I think it is important to know this. Some extremely intelligent strategists have suggested that the Russians are manufacturing over 1,000 planes capable of making a one way flight. I think there are 100 to 200 which are long range planes capable of getting back again. However, it is suggested that over 1,000 planes can make a one way flight, and that is all that would be necessary.
The minister himself has suggested that the number of megaton bombs that could be dropped on the United States is unlimited, but he says he feels that the ability to drop them is limited. To what extent is it limited? This is what I want to know. He gave us some very interesting figures on the difference between a one megaton bomb and a five megaton bomb and he said that a five megaton bomb is not five times as effective as a one megaton bomb. There is no escalation in the price. A five megaton bomb is not five times more expensive or five times heavier. Therefore it is quite feasible that an aeroplane could carry 1 of these 100 megaton or super bombs, as has been suggested.
It seems to me that until we know what the absolute threat is, we cannot play our part. I realize that we are doing this in conjunction with our allies, but just how effective are we in this whole matter? If the Russians have 1,000 planes, one strategist suggests; that at least two thirds would get through. In the last war they were lucky to get 10 per cent through. But let us suppose that even with the much better bombers they have today and with the defence that is put up, 50 per cent get through. On this basis, in an all-out nuclear war, that would be enough to completely annihilate every single person on the North American continent.


I think the problem is that we must have some idea of what this danger is. I humbly appeal to the Minister of National Defence and to his department to tell the Canadian people just exactly what the threat is. What I am concerned about is the tremendous amount of propaganda that is coming out -I will not say it is from the Pentagon-to the effect that we can survive a nuclear war. Yet it has been suggested by the strategist whom I have quoted that there is no such possibility, no matter what kind of shelter we have or what emergency measures organization.
Perhaps I will be accused-and I hope that this will not be the case-of being childish and trying to scare people. I do not think this is the point at all. In a democracy I think if a danger exists we should have the truth. If it is suggested that the people cannot be told the truth because they would lose their compulsion or desire to fight, then I suggest that democracy has lost before the first missile has been launched.
I hope the minister will answer a few of these questions I have in this regard. To what extent is Russia armed with missiles that may be delivered by ICBM or by submarine? Perhaps along with that question I might ask this one, and here again I realize we are not trying to fight Russia by ourselves. Assuming the Russian determination, resources and technological skill which are quite evident from their research into space, how many years, will it be before they have enough missiles so they will be able to foresake bombers completely, and before the Bomarcs and other material we are using will be completely out of date? Can he give us any information in this area?

First of all, the hon. member said he wanted the truth. I should like to emphasize the fact that every statement I make in regard to this matter is truthful as far as the facts at my disposal are concerned. I would not think of telling the hon. member or the Canadian public as a whole anything but the truth in regard to these matters.
The general situation is this. We know that the Russians possess a very considerable number of nuclear weapons. We know they have a large fleet of submarines. We believe they perhaps have some submarines that are capable of firing nuclear tipped missiles. As I say, we believe this is probably the situation; of course we do not know the order of battle of the entire Russian army, navy and air force. We naturally receive some intelligence reports in connection with this. I think the hon. member will realize, however, that it would not be in the interests of

this country to state what the various intelligence estimates are from time to time as to Russian capabilities in certain of these things.
The statement I have made on several occasions previously and which I should like to repeat is that as far as air attack on this continent is concerned, we believe, and we think we have good reason for believing, that the number of intercontinental missiles which the Russians have and which would be available for delivery on this continent is quite limited. On the other hand, they have a very large fleet of both medium and long range bombers. Therefore in the event of a full scale nuclear war the appreciation is that the main weight of the attack would be delivered by these bombers.
The hon. member has said that, of course, in the last war a considerable number of bombers always got through. I said two days ago, I think, in this debate that naturally you cannot have a perfect defence against bombers or, as far as that goes, against almost anything else. But if your defence is sufficiently strong, that in itself constitutes a very strong deterrent to the use of these bombers, missiles or anything else. In other words, if we have sufficiently strong forces in the western world we thereby, in my view at least, greatly diminish the chances of attack. This is really the basis and the theory upon which the NATO alliance has been working, that if we maintain sufficiently strong forces, both nuclear and conventional, the chance of war is very much diminished because it would result in mutual destruction.
I do not think I can answer the hon. member's questions any better than that. I do not know if this is what he was trying to get at, but this is the situation as we see it.

speechtext:
The minister has made a plea for responsibility and accuracy in statements on this important matter, and I agree that this is of first importance. I find it difficult not to remind him of some statements which he himself has made and which contravene that principle, including his statement in Victoria as reported that the Arrow would have cost $15 million a plane.
I also wish to refer, because I think it should be corrected, to a statement which was made by the minister last evening and reported on page 8402 of Hansard with regard to Liberal policy on air defence and particularly continental air defence. The hon. gentleman said that the policy they have been stating since-"they" being the Liberal party, and "since" being last January-is that we do not need interceptors; we should have only a few airplanes for reconnaissance and identification purposes, but they should not shoot. The minister will have a hard time, I think, finding statements which I have made as the leader of this party since that time which would confirm that statement.
We have said that the number of interceptor squadrons, the number of continental air defence squadrons, should be reduced. I think I said it should be reduced to five or six squadrons. Well, the government itself have done this. They are, I understand, disbanding four of the nine squadrons, so the continental air defence force in this country will consist of five squadrons instead of nine. I do not know whether or not the minister considers that number to be sufficient for the purpose; I do not know whether he considers that to be only a "few" airplanes, but the number has been reduced.
Then we have said that we should not try to deceive anybody, especially our own people, by saying that those squadrons, especially squadrons of CF-100's-because that is what we were talking about at that time- could do anything to protect this country against the kind of jet bomber which now faces us if there should be war; because those particular planes, however effective


they may have once been and however skilfully operated, could not intercept the latest jet bombers. The minister confirmed that this morning. So there would be no protection from planes of that kind. They are to be replaced now by a plane which is no longer in production in the United States but which, the minister says, will be effective for this purpose.
We have said, without trying to deceive our people as to what can be done that there should be five or six squadrons-and we shall now have five-of the latest type of planes for reconnaissance, identification, tracking and interception of isolated intruders, capable, if necessary, of dealing with them. This is the only effective role which can now be performed, as we see it, by the R.C.A.F. in this sphere. I am not talking about other important roles on which the R.C.A.F. should be employed.
Then the minister went on to attribute to us the statement that they should not fire. I have more than once in the last six months said that of course any planes being sent into the air for such a purpose would have to be armed, but that they should not be armed with nuclear weapons, because this would be too high a price to pay for bringing Canada into the nuclear club. That is our position on this matter. The minister has been talking about the threat which faces us, and so has the hon. member for Peterborough. The minister has reaffirmed this morning that the Arrow was too expensive a plane for the purpose we had in mind, and I agree with the hon. gentleman that it does not get us much further if we rethresh that old straw. But because I think it is of first importance in assessing this problem, together with what was done and what was not done to solve it, I put on record again the words of the then minister of national defence on February 23, 1959, as reported on page 1280 of Hansard, when he said:
It would therefore not seem to make sense for us to go ahead and develop an interceptor which would be ready by the end of 1961 and which could be in squadron operation by the end of 1962, to meet a threat which would hardly exist at that time.
"That time" is 1962. We are purchasing these planes, or at any rate we are acquiring them from the United States-planes which are new to us but which are out of production in the United States now-to meet a threat which the minister of defence told us some years ago would hardly exist in 1962. That is the position.
As the hon. member for Peterborough has said, we on this side do not know all the facts of the situation. We do not have the

information which is available to the minister. That is one of the handicaps under which we must labour, and we have had no defence committee this year which would enable us to ascertain such facts as were available. The minister said yesterday, and he has said many times, that this was our fault because we were given a chance to debate this subject. And so we were, about a year ago, or ten months or so ago. We were given it at a time when the Prime Minister could not be here, and on a short day. That was to be our debate on defence. The fact that we did not have a debate on defence that day is surely no answer to our criticism that since that time there should have been a committee set up to deal with these matters so that we might get all the facts which are available.
The hon. member for Peterborough asked about some of these things, including the nature of the threat which faces us from the air, the quantity and quality of the bombers and missiles which constitute that threat, and all the rest of it. The minister has said that for security reasons it would be improper for him to give us that information. Well, the hon. gentleman must be the judge of that. We do not quarrel with him on that point. Nobody wants to have information which would prejudice our security, though we do not need to apologize for asking questions. But I would remind the minister, and he must know this, that a great deal of this information is given in Washington including details, in so far as they have been ascertained, of the nature of the bomber threat which faces this continent. Any member of this committee can read chapter after chapter, blue book after blue book of evidence given, for instance, to the house committee on defence appropriations and get a great deal of detailed information which we do not have at our disposal in this chamber. If we did have that information perhaps we should be in a better position to discuss these questions.
I have some detailed questions which perhaps I could address to the minister at this time. They arise out of passages in the blue book which I have before me. I should like to ask what role will be performed in Europe by those four squadrons which are not being converted. The minister tells us that the CF-100 is not now capable of performing the role in continental defence which was given to it. Are the CF-100 squadrons, or they may be Sabre squadrons, capable of performing their role with NATO? Also, with respect to the F-104 aircraft for the new role of strike attack, is it a fact, as stated by experts, including General Foulkes-who of course is not responsible for government policy and is
Supply-National Defence not speaking in any official capacity when he now talks or writes-that the F-104 aircraft cannot perform effectively the role of strike attack without carrying what have been referred to, among others by the NATO commander, as baby nuclear bombs?

Mr. Chairman, the Leader of the Opposition made some complaint about the statement I made to the effect that the Liberal party had withdrawn from the position taken at their national meeting. I am very glad they have, as a matter of fact. According to the newspapers they adopted a resolution at that meeting which, in effect, urged that we should stop wasting our defence resources on interceptor fighter squadrons and on Bomarc missiles, that although the United States with its vast resources and world responsibilities might find these forms of defence necessary there was no reason for Canada participating in that role in these circumstances.
Yes.

The Liberal party went on record as being against having any fighter squadrons. As I stated, the Leader of the Opposition has since modified that position. I am glad he has modified it. I feel he has now adopted a much more realistic position.
The hon. member referred to a statement made two years ago or more by the former minister in connection with the diminishing bomber threat. Whatever might have been said by him at that time, the present situation is that we are confronted with a bomber threat. All western governments recognize that it exists and are taking measures to counter it. Despite what might have been said two years ago or more about anybody's appreciation of the situation at that time, it is at the present situation we must look.
I believe the Leader of the Opposition recognizes that the recent Moscow air show was a demonstration of the fact that the Russians have been continuing to build planes of modern design, contrary to what perhaps might have been thought two or three years ago, would be the situation. Actually the development of the so-called stand-off bomber, the air to surface missile carried by a bomber, has undoubtedly considerably prolonged the useful life of bombers. That is one reason that led to a considerable modification of the thinking of two or three years ago in regard to bombers.
The Leader of the Opposition wished to know about the role of the CF-100 in Europe, the four squadrons which are not being replaced by F-104's. SACEUR has requested that these squadrons remain there for at least two more years to meet an existing need. As far as the strike reconnaissance role of the

Supply-National Defence F-104 is concerned, both SACEUR and the NATO council have asked Canada to assume this role with respect to the eight squadrons presently armed with Sabre aircraft which are now to be rearmed with the F-104. We have met that request.
The Leader of the Opposition asked if they would not be useless in that role unless armed with nuclear weapons. I believe that was the purport of the hon. gentleman's question.
Yes.

That is not the case. They could be armed otherwise and be effective to some extent, but there is no question but that they would be much more effective if equipped with nuclear warheads, just as in the case of the Bomarc and other weapons systems which are capable of carrying nuclear warheads. I think this is not an arguable matter. If you have a conventional warhead which has a force of one, and a nuclear warhead of the same size which has a force of one hundred, the nuclear warhead will be very much more effective. That is a plain fact. The situation with respect to F-104's is that they would be much more effective and destructive weapons if armed with nuclear warheads rather than conventional rockets.

Mr. Chairman, may I thank the minister for the information he has given. He has stated, and undoubtedly it is a fact, that while the former minister of defence spoke in 1959 and said the bomber threat would not likely exist to any extent in 1962, that situation has changed. A major factor which led the government to the decision it made in regard to air defence in 1959 turned out to be wrong in that the bomber threat, according to the minister, does exist, and it exists in an aggravated form perhaps because of what the minister has called the stand-off bomber by which a missile can be carried and let loose on a target, we have been informed, up to 1,000 miles away.
There is a difference of opinion on that. The minister says that range is too high. The information we have received indicates that if it is not now the range, it will be shortly. This, of course, establishes an entirely different set of conditions for continental defence against the bomber. The threat comes no longer from the bomber but from the missile which is capable of being discharged from a bomber at a distance of from 400 to 1,000 miles away from the target.
Presumably the government has had to modify its policy to meet that changed situation, and modification is a good thing when conditions change. I wish to assure the minister, however, that this party has not


changed its policy with respect to continental defence, to which the minister made reference. We have not changed our minds. We should not be engaged in continental defence with the United States continental air defence command in a way which would necessitate Canada becoming a member of the nuclear club.
That, of course, applies both to interceptor squadrons and to the Bomarc missile. If it were felt on this side of the house that such weapons were absolutely essential for the protection of this country, this continent and the strategic air bases, that perhaps would not be too high a price to pay, although it would be very high. But this is not essential in our view, and therefore we should not be performing this role. While we would advocate a fighting role in the sense that the planes would be armed and in the sense that Canadians could not allow Americans to do the fighting and shooting for them, Canada's role should not be a fighting role, in the sense that the planes need not be armed with nuclear weapons; because we do not think that this would be necessary in view of the changing nature of the threat; if such a threat is going to make Bomarcs and other weapons of that kind ineffective very shortly if they are not ineffective now.
That is the situation, and we have not modified our stand in that regard. I have made it quite clear, however, that we think the squadrons the R.C.A.F. should have should be the most effective and efficient that can be secured in terms of equipment, and they certainly should be in a position to defend themselves.
With respect to another question I directed to him, the minister said that while the F-104 could perform a role without what are described as baby nuclear bombs, that role would not be of maximum effectiveness without such nuclear weapons, and we can leave it at that.

Mr. Chairman, in view of what the Leader of the Opposition has said about stand-off bombers, the size and range of the missiles which they might discharge and so on, and in view of what was said yesterday about them, I think I should quote an extract from page 12 of the testimony of the secretary of defence of the United States before the subcommittee of the committee on appropriations in April of 1961. This was his statement at that time:
Also under development Is a more advanced air to ground missile, the Skybolt. This is a solid fuel ballistic missile with a design range of about 1,000 miles. Whereas the B-52 can carry only two Hound Dog missiles, it would be able to carry four Skybolt missiles. The successful development of an effective Skybolt missile would offset the

expected increase in Soviet air defence capabilities by increasing the effective attack radius of a B-52 and the penetration capability of its weapons, as well as increasing its ability to launch stand-off attacks on multiple targets. However, the Skybolt is a costly project and presents some unusually complex development problems. Even if the development is successful, it would take several years to bring it to operational status.
The hon. member for Trinity contended yesterday that this missile was in existence or would exist shortly, but the fact is that it does not exist. As the United States secretary of defence says, it presents a very difficult development problem, and even if the development is successful it will be several years before it will be in operation.

I thank the minister for that explanation. As he probably realizes, elsewhere in the same testimony it is indicated that the total SAGE-Bomarc system will not be in operation in its entirety for several years either, and the time lapse, if that is the proper term for it, is approximately the same in each case.
If I understood the minister correctly, he indicated that the bomber threat is more substantial than it was two or three years ago. He told us the night before last, I believe, that he did not say it was not diminishing, but this morning he gives the impression that the facts today are different from what they were then, and that as a result of the facts existing today the government should take some action to meet this threat even though earlier it was not considered to be required.
If the threat is greater today than was anticipated, why are the government only acquiring 66 planes, when earlier their appraisal was somewhat different even on the basis of their then belief that the bomber threat was not so great? As found on page 1281 of Hansard for February 23, 1959 the former minister had this to say:
We therefore concluded that the maximum number of aircraft that we would require to meet the threat would be approximately 100 ...
If the threat is greater now, or is interpreted by the government as being greater now, why will 66 planes do more work now than 100 planes were estimated to be able to accomplish at that time?

There is no magic in the figure 66 or in the figure 100 in connection with this particular matter. The important point is that with the "Sageing" of the whole NORAD system, which incidentally will be completed in 1963, the means of employing the Bomarc chain and the interceptors of both the United States and Canada is very greatly improved, and therefore the capability of the whole system is much higher than it was two
Supply-National Defence years ago or three years ago. It has been constantly improved every year, in fact, and the ability of the system both to detect and then to direct on hostile intruders either Bomarc missiles or interceptor planes has been getting better and better all the time.
Therefore, as I say, there is no particular magic in 66 planes or 100 planes. You have an integrated system making use of the air defence command of Canada and the air defence command of the United States under the operational control of NORAD, and with constantly improving methods of employing those forces in order to destroy intruder aircraft.

With respect to the cost of operating the Pine Tree line, the minister told us this morning that the committee would have to accept the figures prepared by responsible officials of the Department of National Defence. Can the minister explain the discrepancy between the figures prepared by responsible officials of the Department of National Defence on a previous occasion and those given to the committee this morning?
I do not know what previous occasion is referred to, Mr. Chairman.
I am referring to the time his predecessor gave figures to the committee on defence expenditures, which presumably were also prepared by_ responsible officials of the Department of National Defence.

I think where the confusion exists with regard to this matter perhaps lies in the fact that General Pearkes quoted a figure of $43 million which, to begin with, included $5 million for equipment to be purchased in Canada. This equipment was new radars. Therefore the actual cost of operation and maintenance was $38 million. However, the $38 million covered not only those radars but also the radars in Newfoundland, the gap fillers and so forth, the nine group one radars and all their associated gap fillers. They were not included in the 11 that we have taken over and the five which we have been manning already, and for which we have assumed financial responsibility.
Can the minister say who is paying for the new heavy radars that are being built?
This is part of a general cost sharing program of one third to Canada and two thirds to the United States. We are doing the construction as our contribution to the cost.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with great interest to the discussion so far this morning, and have attempted to follow

Supply-National Defence the minister's comments and statements. In order to have the matter clear perhaps I might give my understanding of his reasoning, and if I am in error in my interpretation of what he said he can correct me.
With respect to the use of the Bomarc, the Voodoo or CF-104 as I believe it is to be called, and perhaps even the Honest John surface to surface missile, I understood him to say that the greatest deterrent that exists to a war being started or visited upon us by enemy forces is if we have a sufficiently strong defence, and that the stronger our defence the greater is the deterrent to attack from other countries. If that is a correct understanding of what the minister said-
It is the retaliatory forces.

This is what I want to get clear. It would seem to me that our defence and the deterrent is not the Bomarc, the rifle or the Honest John or any other kind of small, tactical weapon of that sort. The deterrent, as the minister has just stated, is the threat of retaliation, which is not something that Canada has. As I understand it, this threat of retaliation rests primarily at the moment in the United States strategic air command. The defence is really one of threatening to bomb the enemy country and do as much damage or more damage than the enemy expects he will be able to do to this country.
If that is a correct understanding, and I thought I had it correctly, then it seems to me that in view of what the minister told us on Wednesday, that NATO is and in fact has been since 1954 a nuclear element, operating on somewhat the same principle of retaliation as a defence more than anything else, Canada really is part of the nuclear club in NATO. It would seem to me that Canada is already part of the nuclear forces on the North American continent, whether or not we have such weapons in the hands of Canadian troops and on Canadian soil. It would seem to me that following this, whether we are in possession of the Bomarc with nuclear warheads or without them, or the Honest John or any other type of rocket with or without nuclear warheads, it really does not matter very much so far as being a deterrent to attack is concerned, because the deterrent rests not in our hands but in the hands of the United States strategic air command.
This is what makes incomprehensible to me the recent statement by the Leader of the Opposition that the acquiring of nuclear warheads by Canada is almost too high a price to pay, regardless of the circumstances, for some sort of defence. The defence rests in the possession by the United States of nuclear


and thermonuclear bombs and in the threat of retaliation, the threat of destruction to other countries. It seems to me that following from that Canada is in precisely the same position on the North American continent as we are in Europe with the NATO forces; that is, that we are already a part of the nuclear club whether we like it or not, and whether or not we have nuclear warheads on Canadian soil attached to Bomarcs or anything else is relatively inconsequential.
The point in so far as the deterrent is concerned is that it is not our deterrent, it is not Canada that is threatening retaliation. The only deterrent that exists, as the minister has said, is in United States miltiary forces that are threatening this sort of retaliation. This is the only defence which exists and is the greatest deterrent to attack. I think we can assume that the same situation applies to the Soviet union. This is substantially their defence or offence policy, whichever way you want to classify it. Any other nation that comes, by its own right or through development, into possession of nuclear weapons will fall into almost the same category.
It would seem to me that the very moment we endorsed the NORAD treaty, which was supported by the Liberal party in this house, we in fact joined the North American nuclear club. Those are forces in the control of or under the domination of the nuclear deterrent in the United States. This makes me wonder even more whether the minister and the Liberal party when they were in office- because the development of the nuclear deterrent was in process then, and it was during their term of office that NATO followed nuclear strategy and the NORAD agreement was spawned and finally came to fruition- were telling a completely factual story of Canada's position in so far as North American defence is concerned. I think it would be much more in keeping with our sense of responsibility to the electorate if the government would make a clear, definite statement as to just precisely where Canada stands.
It is my interpretation, following from what the minister has said and in this I may be incorrect, that Canada is in fact a participant in a nuclear agency, NATO. If that is the case, and I take it that it is, it seems to me also that Canada is a participant in another nuclear agency, namely that of the United States, primarily through our participation in NORAD. If these are the facts then they should be stated clearly to the Canadian public. There should not be any of this nonsense, and I term it nonsense in retrospect, of people in high places in this government talking about no nuclear weapons in the hands of Canadian troops; no nuclear weapons on Canadian soil, then changing

later to say that there might be, depending on what arrangements we can work out with the United States and depending on what congress does with certain laws that exist down there. In my opinion this is all just a lot of double talk on the part of the government. If my interpretation is not correct, then I should like the minister to straighten it out.
Stated again, not for repetition only but just so it is clear, it is my understanding following upon what the minister stated that Canada really has no defence in terms of being a deterrent to attack; that that sort of defence of deterrence and prevention of invasion or attack by another country rests on the retaliatory force of the United States, primarily their bomber squadrons in the strategic air command; that Canada, particularly as a participant in NORAD, is in almost the same boat as she is in NATO, and that is that we are participants in a nuclear agency because we have in fact joined forces with the United States and its military forces.
If my interpretation is incorrect, I should like to have the minister clear it up. If it is correct, then I think a clear, unequivocal statement should be made to the Canadian public so we are not led down the garden path by the Prime Minister or anybody else talking about "no nuclear weapons on Canadian soil as long as I am Prime Minister", and all this other business.

First of all, the Prime Minister has never made any statement along that line. I do not think the hon. member should be making allegations of that kind without producing any proof of them whatever. I certainly have never seen or heard of any declaration along that line by the Prime Minister at any time.
I should like to make it clear that the deterrent consists of several elements. The deterrent is not merely the nuclear capability of the strategic air command of the United States, their intercontinental ballistic missiles, their Polaris submarines and the V-bomber force of Great Britain. These are the nuclear parts of the deterrent. They are the part of the deterrent which would respond to or retaliate or actually deliver nuclear weapons to Russian territory if the Russians attacked us. But the deterrent is made up of much more than that. It consists of all the defensive air measures which we take in order to ensure that as few as possible enemy bombers would be able to reach targets in the NATO countries. It consists also of all of the conventional forces. It consists of all the naval forces. In other words the entire military forces of the western world constitute the deterrent, not just the one part of them which would be used to drop bombs. It is an
Supply-National Defence integrated whole. The greater the strength of the armed forces as a whole, the greater the deterrent power we have and the more unlikely it is that the Russians would start a war.
That is the basic situation as far as the deterrent is concerned. You cannot isolate one part only and say it is the deterrent. If you had the SAC air force and some intercontinental ballistic missiles only and had no conventional forces to protect them, and no interceptor aircraft, radar warning lines and so forth, they would not last very long and they would not constitute very much of a deterrent. Actually the deterrent is not only what you have in peacetime but what the enemy think you will have left after he actually attacks you. This is where the striking part of the deterrent becomes so important.
The hon. member said that we had placed our forces under the control of the United States by entering into the NORAD agreement. As I have made clear in this debate and on many other occasions, this is not the case. The NORAD agreement was a means of co-ordinating the air defence command of Canada and the air defence command of the United States in order to get the quickest possible reaction time to any threat. In the event of attack it provided for operational control of these defence forces by a co-ordinated headquarters in which the commander is a United States general and the second in command is a Canadian air marshal. When the commander, General Kuter, is away from the Colorado Springs headquarters, as he is quite frequently, Air Marshal Slemon is in full command of the NORAD operation.
No control of Canadian forces has been given to the United States by entering into this agreement. It is a mutual undertaking. As I say, command is exercised by officers of both countries. At the headquarters in Colorado Springs, as is realized by those who have been there, there are officers from both countries and they are doing all kinds of different jobs. It is a fully integrated headquarters, with no distinction being made whether it is a Canadian in a particular job or whether it is an American. There is a good deal of changing around in the jobs from time to time as people's tours of duty come to an end and other people replace them.
I think the Prime Minister and I myself have been quite clear and quite plain in stating what is the position of Canada in connection with NATO, the NORAD agreement and the defence situation generally. I therefore think there is no justification for any allegations of double talk on the part of the government with regard to these matters. These are serious matters. I have made every effort to try to keep the public

Supply-National Defence informed as well as I could as to what the situation was, at least as I saw it.

I wonder whether I could ask of the minister a very short question arising out of a story appearing in the London Times of September 9. Under date of September 8 from Ottawa the correspondent of the Times says this:
But what is particularly in people's minds here now is whether Canada will be forced to accept nuclear warheads for her Bomarc missile weapons in Ontario and Quebec . ..
I wonder whether I might respectfully ask the minister if he could give us an answer and call it one o'clock, or perhaps he has an immediate answer?

I presume this is an article by some correspondent, Mr. Chairman. I do not know what answer I can give to it. This is speculation. I can see no answer that I can give to speculation on the part of a correspondent of the London Times.

Before you call it one o'clock, Mr. Chairman, perhaps I could ask the minister one question to which he may reply after one o'clock or perhaps immediately, as it is a very simple and direct one. Can the minister tell us whether there is in existence, awaiting signature by the government of Canada, a draft agreement for the joint control of nuclear weapons?
I am sorry to disappoint the curiosity of the hon. member.
Carried.
