speechtext: Order. Shall vote 239 carry?
Mr. Chairman, would the minister indicate whether the department did try to obtain an off-the-shelf price for the Voodoo aircraft, and if so, how much was it? Was it a cash price?

Mr. Chairman, we did not ask for any off-the-shelf price in regard to this airplane. The cost of the airplane to the United States government was in the neighbourhood of $1.6 million a copy, I believe. That was a fly away price, without any spares, supporting equipment and so forth.
Could the minister say with what missile the Voodoo will be equipped?
The Falcon missile.
Will that be the only missile it will carry?
No, the Voodoo can carry another type of missile, the MB-1, which is a nuclear weapon. The Falcon is a conventional warhead weapon.
Will it carry the Sidewinder as well as the Falcon?
No.
Will the hardware on the airplane be such that it will take the MB-1?
That is what I said a minute ago. It can carry the MB-1 as well as the Falcon.
And that hardware will be on the airplanes which the R.C.A.F. is securing?
We are securing Falcons for the airplanes.
I think the minister understood what I was asking for. That was, whether or not the attachments from which the other missile would be launched would be on the airplane as procured.

Yes. Perhaps I might explain that these missiles are launched from the airplane on a sort of table which can be turned. On one side are the attachments for the Falcon and on the other side are the attachments for the MB-1.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if I might bring a matter to the attention of the minister very briefly, and perhaps down from the high level of international commitments to the level of the local taxpayer, and specifically the taxpayer in my district.
The problem arises from the defence installations now being constructed in our area; in particular, SAGE at the Trout lake site. Early last year there was an announcement, as a committee will recall, that 200 homes would be built in that area to accommodate personnel at this military installation.
Some discussions have taken place among the local municipality, the local school board and the minister's department. I have here a letter dated May 19 this year from the chief of air staff to Mr. A. J. Norman, business administrator for the township school area of Widdifield. One passage of this letter reads as follows:
On the basis of 200 additional homes this could mean a requirement for Widdifield township to accommodate 340 elementary pupils-
The letter then goes on to deal with high school pupils, etc. The situation is that our

municipality, like other municipalities, is very heavily burdened, particularly in the field of providing facilities for education. To point up the problem, last year when we were examining the estimates of the Department of Public Works the minister indicated, as reported at page 6853 of Hansard for June 21, that the total housing requirement would be 575 units. On the basis of the figures of the Department of National Defence this would indicate a requirement for accommodation for almost 1,000 students at the elementary school level. The department is using-I was going to say "hiding behind"-the contention that the responsibility rests upon the local authority. Here again I should like to quote these words from a further letter from the chief of the air staff to the business administrator in the area:
However, as the proposed 200 additional housing units will not be constructed on federal property, the financing of providing and maintaining any additional school facilities for the occupants of those units is regarded by this headquarters as the responsibility of the municipality or township, in exactly the same manner as for other new civilian property ratepayers not necessarily employed by the R.C.A.F.
This is all very fine, and the department can retreat behind regulations of this type but, surely, the wise administration of any department calls for a high degree of common sense. Surely, in the light of the developments which are taking place in the area there is need for a further look at situations of this kind. As I said, we have been pursuing this subject with the department. My purpose in bringing the matter to the minister's attention today is to soften him up, because this problem will have to be met. The construction of 200 homes was announced last year. A second announcement later in the year spoke of 575 homes. The minister will correct me if I am wrong, but I believe current plans call for something in the order of 350 homes, 100 of which may be out for tender this month. There is another group off the station property itself and a further, third, block making up a total of some 350 homes which will probably be occupied by the end of 1962. Without pursuing the matter further here and delaying the committee, may I say that I hope the minister can tell us the exact requirements of the department as far as housing in this area is concerned and give us some assurance that representatives of his department will meet with our board to deal with this important problem.

Two types of housing are being referred to here. The first concerns the houses on the station itself and, of course, we have provided a school and are looking after the education of the children occupying those
Supply-National Defence houses. Then there are the houses being built in the town under a rental housing agreement just as there are low cost housing developments in various other cities across the country under the central mortgage and housing corporation. The houses which are being built in the town are being built so that they may be rented to the people who will be working at this station. They are in the same category as houses built for rental in other places. Taxes will be paid with respect to them, and these taxes contribute to the upkeep of the local schools and other facilities. As a result, the children of the people who live in the houses are entitled to go to the local schools.

So that there may be no misunderstanding about this, let me say that what the minister has told the committee is correct as far as it goes. But only a small portion of the homes to be built in the area is being built on national defence property. The great bulk of them will be built in the small local municipality, which has just completed an extensive program of providing new school accommodation and which may now be faced, according to the figures which are available, with the cost of providing school accommodation for a thousand additional students. I hope the minister will bear this in mind because the situation cannot be passed off as being the same as a situation arising from a housing development of any other kind. This burden has been dropped in our laps to accommodate the people who are to be absorbed by this defence installation. Some consideration will have to be given to assisting in the provision of the capital cost of providing these facilities and I hope the minister will bear that in mind when we pursue our representations in this regard.

There is one matter which I should like to raise with the minister. It was referred to me by a constituent, formerly a member of the R.C.A.F., who was stationed at the air station of St. Sylvestre, near Quebec city. I am not altogether familiar with the arrangements laid down for what are called non-public funds but I understand they are funds in the nature of canteen funds and the like. A number of projects are set up which give servicemen an opportunity to earn extra money and do interesting work in their leisure hours. I think that this is perhaps a good way of keeping the men interested and giving people associated with the service certain amenities which perhaps otherwise would not be available.
However, my informant advises me that in the air station at St. Sylvestre, which is one of the Pine Tree Stations, there is not only a

Supply-National Defence gas station where n.c.o.'s are employed full time to pump gas but also a grocery store where a flight sergeant, who is paid flight sergeant's pay, operates full time. I am also told that there is a snack bar and gift shop which, until recently, has been operating full time staffed by service personnel, in addition to a post office which was formerly operated by a civilian but which has recently been taken over by air force personnel. Most of these men, I am told, are skilled tradesmen in receipt of trade pay in addition to their regular pay and allowances as members of the air force but they are not performing air force duties, nor are they working at trades for which they receive extra remuneration.
My informant advises me that one of the reasons for this situation is that the chief administrative officer is in charge of the nonpublic funds and is responsible for detailing men from various sections to take jobs in connection with the non-public funds amenities available. This strikes me as being an improper practice. I cannot myself take responsibility for all these facts because I have not been in the area myself. However, my informant was stationed there and he tells me this has been going on for a protracted period. I should like the minister to tell us whether this is a proper practice or not, and how this situation has come into being. If it is not a proper practice perhaps he would have an inquiry made.

The regulations of the
R.C.A.F. in this regard are very strict. No R.C.A.F. personnel are to be employed in non-public fund operations in duty hours. If they are being employed, they are being improperly employed. I do not know what the situation is at this particular station at St. Sylvestre. I have never heard any complaints of this nature with regard to the station before, but I shall have an investigation made and see if there is any validity in these allegations.

I wonder if the minister could tell us whether any of the CF-100 squadrons presently under air defence command will be retained in service or whether they will all be phased out as the Voodoo comes into service.
It is intended to retain some of the CF-lOO's in the electronic warfare school and for some other purposes, but not as interceptors.
Not as complete squadrons?
No.

The minister indicated this morning that the squadrons overseas equipped

with CF-lOO's would remain in service until the end of 1961 or 1962, I believe.
Could the minister say whether he has any plans to replace them at that time and, more particularly, with the F-101B?
No definite plans have been worked out as to what action might be taken to replace the CF-lOO's at that time.

With respect to the F-104
could the minister say when the first squad-dons will be posted overseas?
In November of 1962.
Have arrangements yet been worked out with the government of France for their operation from French air bases in the event they are equipped with atomic arms?
No, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I was waiting for the appropriate item to be called but since I have been given the floor I should like to say a few words in praise of the R.C.A.F. While attending the war memorial celebrations in France last July I had an opportunity to make a brief visit to the air base at Marville. I was very much impressed by the way this unit was being run. I am sure the people of Canada have every reason to be proud of the R.C.A.F. units which are representing Canada overseas.
We were conveyed back and forth by the R.C.A.F. jet transport. At this point I should also like to say a few words of appreciation of that unit. We were treated with the utmost courtesy and consideration and were provided a meal in transit which compares very favourably with meals provided on commercial aircraft. When we reached the end of our journey we were provided with a card on which we were asked to note our suggestions concerning improvement of the service and I was unable to think of any way in which it could be improved.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to join with my hon. friend in that tribute. We have an air force second to none. It is too bad that it has had to go so long since the proud days of 1955 and 1956 without new equipment. We also regret, as said before, that it is undertaking a new role of strike reconnaissance rather than having ground support fighter aircraft to back up the Canadian troops there.
Could the minister say what types of helicopter are being obtained by the air force and what they have available in Europe for support of the army when required?

The R.C.A.F. is obtaining some Vertol helicopters. This is a medium to heavy helicopter which will be used, particularly in Canada, for search and rescue. They are obtaining also, of course, some light helicopters.
Is the Vertol the twin rotor helicopter that looks like an inverted banana?
It is the Vertol-107. I cannot say anything with respect to the description of an inverted banana. I think most helicopters look somewhat like that.
Could the minister indicate the type of light helicopter the air force is obtaining? Is it the same one the army is receiving?
Yes.

Could the minister tell the committee if the figures concerning the completion of homes used in the schedule to which I referred are in agreement with the latest figures he has available? I purposely delayed pursuing that to give the officials an opportunity to check it.
I have not yet received those figures but I shall give them to the hon. member in a few moments.

The minister indicated earlier today that most of the air transport aircraft would be in service by the end of this calendar year. Can the minister say how many of those currently on order will be available by then, if any?
The Yukons have all been delivered. They are undergoing flight testing and so on. I believe I said that they would be in full operation or full squadron use by the end of the year.
Has the minister any plans to augment the transport command beyond those presently funded?

We have some projected plans but nothing has been definitely authorized so far. Of course, the retention of the North Stars in service which was announced this week means that the whole transport capability of the R.C.A.F. is now very much greater and will continue much greater than it has ever been before.

Will the minister explain to the committee how the Caribou aircraft which was purchased in haste and delivered under such pressure by the de Havilland aircraft company for use in the Congo wound up in the Gaza strip?

All I can say is that in the final analysis it was decided they were not
Supply-National Defence needed in the Congo and the United Nations wanted them in the Gaza strip.

Can the minister say whether any Canadian minister wrote the Secretary General of the United Nations asking that the Caribou be used only by Canadian troops and received the reply that that was not a condition satisfactory to the United Nations?
I cannot say that, no.

Now that the Prime Minister has entered the chamber perhaps I could address this question to him. Can the Prime Minister say whether any representations were made on behalf of Canada to the United Nations that, first, the Caribou aircraft be used only by Canadian troops in the Congo or, second, that Canadian troops be given a preference in their use over other troops, and was this condition rejected by the United Nations? Is that the reason the Caribou aircraft were not used in the Congo by the United Nations forces?
Mr. Chairman, I cannot add anything to what has already been placed before the committee by the Minister of National Defence.

Can the Minister of National Defence explain then why he would require employees from an aircraft company to give up the week which had been set apart for their holidays and to rush back to the aircraft factory to deliver aircraft which sat on the ramps at Trenton for weeks or months before they were used for anything?
All I can say is that the situation in the Congo, as all hon. gentlemen opposite are well aware, has been changing very rapidly from week to week and in some cases, in fact, from day to day.
It is a fact then, is it, that the Canadian government made no representations to the United Nations with regard to the use of this particular aircraft?
Well, Mr. Chairman, if any representations were made they were not made by me.
I think that is correct. Perhaps the minister would not care to disclose whom they were made by-
I did not say they were made. I said that as far as I am concerned none was made.

I said I believed that. Would the minister indicate why, at a time when we are under such pressure and tension and it is the policy of the government to expand the auxiliary forces and to train 100,000 new men for civil survival purposes, it is also

Supply-National Defence the policy of the Department of National Defence to disband existing auxiliary squadrons of the R.C.A.F. which, although they have had a different function in the past, might conceivably be converted to carry out some useful civil survival role?

The R.C.A.F. auxiliary squadrons, the disbandment of which was decided upon over a year ago and which has been going on for some considerable time, were aircraft warning and control squadrons whose function had disappeared. There was no other function that could be assigned to them at the present time and therefore in the interests of efficiency and economy the only thing that we really could do was to disband them. We were very regretful about having to disband these squadrons but there was really no function that could be given to them which would have added to the defence strength of the country. That was why, very regretfully, the decision was arrived at to disband them.

On the basis of this theory of efficiency and economy, would the minister explain why one branch of the armed services is discharging people and disbanding units at the same time that other branches of the armed services are recruiting and training for other roles? Presumably there might be a possibility of retraining or readaptation.

All I can say is that we would be very glad to welcome all of the members of the squadrons being disbanded into the survival operations and the militia who are carrying out that role. The point is that the survival role in Canada has been given to the army and the militia is carrying a large part of the load in that regard. It is for that reason that we are giving special militia survival training to 100,000 men in order to increase the number of men available with training in survival operations. It would not be a reasonable proposition to be trying to give some sort of role to an air force squadron here, there or some place else when these squadons operate in a completely different manner.
Apparently the minister has not achieved that state of integration yet in the Department of National Defence under which men can be transferred from role to role as required.
As I said, these men can transfer quite readily into the militia units. We would be glad to have them.

The minister will recall that when the BMEWS was first put into operation an alleged false alarm was reported in the newspapers. Can the minister say whether there have been any recurrences of this

type of occupational hazard and can he give the committee any assurance that there are adequate precautions so that a general alarm would not result?
I think the short answer to that is that it was an alleged false alarm but it was not actually a false alarm.
That was the exact phrase I used. I assume from the minister's answer that he is confident that a false alarm cannot in fact occur.

I am confident that it is extremely unlikely it will occur. Whether it is completely impossible for it to occur I am not competent to say. I feel quite certain, however, that no matter what the particular radars or recording screens might happen to show with regard to such an instance it would be well checked in other ways before any action was taken.

Has the minister received any representations from Canadian personnel serving at Goose Bay in respect of the allegation that they are required to use other than Canadian legal tender to make purchases at the United States air force base there?
I have no information on that.

Would the minister agree to look into that situation? I have received representations to the effect that since the Canadian dollar was devalued payment not only at the PX but other local stores is required to be made in United States funds and the Canadian civilians feel that this is an infringement of their rights and probably of their pride and pocketbooks as well. Would the minister undertake to investigate and see if the situation can be corrected?
Yes, I will be glad to.

Mr. Chairman, the minister knows, of course, that the situation in France with regard to the use of French bases for American air equipment with nuclear weapons is such that these bases are not now available to the United States air force. Has there been any indication of a change in that situation that he may know about and has he any reason to believe that the French government will adopt a different position with respect to the Canadian air force if that air force should be equipped with nuclear weapons?

I am not aware of any change in that position except that I noted in the newspapers the other day that some French units were going to be trained by the Americans in the use of nuclear weapons. This might well portend a change but I do not know.

With regard to the number of rental units and housing units generally at North Bay, may I say to the hon. member for Nipissing that there are under consideration 100 permanent married quarters for the station. Two hundred rental units have been approved and a further 200 rental units are under consideration.

I should like to ask the minister to clarify the statement he just made in reply to the question about an alarm. The impression I got from listening to the minister's reply was that it was a genuine alarm and if that was not the case I think it should be made quite clear on Hansard.

The actual situation was that the system was really under test at the time. It had not been taken into full operational use. They began to get reflections from the moon, I believe it was, and this information was of course passed down the line. The way it was portrayed in the newspapers, however, made it appear that it was interpreted as an actual attack and that it was just by a hair's breadth that retaliatory action was not ordered. All that part of the story was completely incorrect.

Item agreed to.
Defence research and development-
Defence research board-
241. Operation and maintenance, $24,993,564.

I should like, first of all, to reiterate what I have said on previous occasions that it is my opinion Canadians are very fortunate in obtaining from the defence research board probably more results for the dollars expended than any other people in the western world. The achievements of this board have been remarkable for the size of the group and the amount of money expended. I should like the minister to indicate whether or not the financial support they are receiving at the present time is greater than in the past or whether he plans to enlarge it and make sure that this extraordinarily fine group is given every possible support in its work.

The amount of money being voted, as is shown in the estimates book, is approximately the same this year as last year. There is no question about what the hon. member has said in regard to the achievements of the defence research board. They have done a remarkably fine job and they are a remarkably good group of scientists. This is an activity of which we can be proud. The board has made great contributions to the defence of this country and of the whole western world and is continuing to do so.
Supply-National Defence

Mr. Chairman, I should like to join with my colleague, the hon. member for Trinity and the minister in paying tribute to the defence research board. I have always had a very special interest in research, particularly in scientific research. Looking back over the years, it seems that the time has come when we should take a good, hard look at our policy in regard to defence research. I have done a little homework in this connection, and I should like to place a few figures on the record. In the year 1950-51, the expenditures on research and development were $23.4 million; in 1951-52, they were $35.4 million; in 1952-53, approximately $43 million; in 1953-54, approximately $41 million; in 1954, approximately $50 million; in 1955, $64 million; in 1956, $69 million; in 1957, $78 million; in 1958, $74 million. Then, in 1959, the figure dropped to $39 million.
All the figures I have mentioned so far have been taken from the public accounts and they are the actual expenditures on research and development. The two figures I want to mention now are estimates taken from the blue book for last year and for the item that is before us at this moment. In 1960, we voted $44.7 million and this year we have in the estimates a vote of just over $45 million. It seems to me that these figures show that since 1958 there has been a significant drop in the amount of money we are allocating to research and development. If we look back over the figures we see there is a steady increase from the $23.4 million in 1950 up to $78 million in 1957, then $74 million in 1958, while in 1959 the figure drops to $39 million and last year and this year is around $45 million. If we add the amounts for the last two years together, we only get a little more than the average of what we have been spending.
It seems to me we are reducing our expenditures on research and development at the very time when we should be increasing them. If there was need to increase them from 1950 to 1958, surely since 1958, with the world situation steadily deteriorating and with an ever-increasing emphasis on scientific development, we cannot hope to keep abreast of the times if we are going to drastically reduce the amount of money we allocate for this purpose. It is all right to praise the achievements of our defence research board, but we cannot expect them to make bricks without straw.
I should like to point out to the minister that the dollars we are giving them today are depreciated dollars. The dollars we are giving them this year have 20 per cent less purchasing power than the dollars we gave them in 1950. We are giving them fewer dollars and a smaller dollar with which to

Supply-National Defence work. We cannot expect them to do credit to Canada or even to their own establishment if we are not going to provide them with the money to enable them to carry on this work.
The minister said in his statement, I think, that the activities of the defence research board would be co-ordinated with industry. I heartily agree with that policy. I think there should be even more co-ordination. I should like to see some authority set up to co-ordinate all research in Canada. We have so many departments now, and practically every department has some research being conducted. Whatever research we may do in defence will always have, for the most part I think, some application in industry. A country like Canada, so dependent upon export trade, certainly should be placing the greatest emphasis on research and development. We should be following the examples of little countries like Switzerland and Sweden who have developed products and techniques that have enabled them to compete with other countries to compensate for their small domestic market.
Let me cite one example, alloys. Alloys are of the utmost importance in defence, particularly with the new weapons and rockets that are coming into use every day. Alloys are of extreme importance in industry as well, in our construction industry and in practically every product of which we can think. I should like to see Canada specialize along certain lines. I understand we have been doing something with regard to equipment for northern climates and also with regard to electronics. It seems that we have been able to take a lead in the electronic research. I realize our resources perhaps are small. But surely here is an opportunity worth embracing. I urge the minister to take another look at this policy and to provide more funds for this extremely important work.

The amount of money spent in research has gone up steadily year by year. The hon. member has taken the two votes together or rather he has taken the two votes for research and then added to them the vote for development. If he will look at the table at the back of the blue book which has a comparison of the expenditures for fiscal years, he will see that, as far as the expenditures of the defence research board are concerned, they have gone up from $23.7 million in 1952-53, to $30.8 million-almost $31 million-estimated for this year, $27 million the year previous and so on. Underneath that is given the development vote and it is quite variable. In some years it showed a figure of $45 million, $53 million, $47 million and so forth. Most of that amount actually was on account of this albatross around our necks.
I refer to the Arrow. It was development work on the Arrow which amounted to these considerable expenditures during those years but it is not part of the research activities. This is development activity.
As far as a program with industry is concerned may I say this. In the speech I made in introducing the estimates I stated that a program of industrial support was being put into effect in conjunction with the Department of Defence Production but under the control of the defence research board. It is designed to do this very thing, namely to assist industry to develop new products and things of that kind.

I thank the minister for the explanation he has given me. It is true that I lumped the two together as I wanted to look back over as many years as possible and I just did not have the time in which to separate out the two figures. However, before coming into the chamber I took the trouble to look at the public accounts for 1960. In that year we allocated $51 million for research and development but we actually spent only $39,183,481. The unspent money I want to point out was for development. We voted $21.5 million that year and actually spent $11.5 million. Hence there was $10.5 million left over. That pattern fairly well holds true for a good part of the period I covered in the figures. I do not know what the situation was last year. Perhaps the minister can tell us exactly what the expenditures were. In last year's blue book we estimated $44,696,364 for research and development. I wonder what the expenditure actually was?

Again, Mr. Chairman, I would have to request the hon. gentleman to separate research from development. They are not the same thing. As I stated, the amount spent on research has been going up steadily year by year whereas the amount spent on development has varied greatly from year to year. If you look at the breakdown of the figures, you will find that the amount spent on development has varied. One year it was $42 million and the next year it was $5 million. You cannot possibly lump these two things together and say it is the amount spent on research. It is not the amount spent on research. The research items are items 241 and 242. The development item is a separate item altogether, namely, item 243. Again in this table at the back of the blue book that was issued it is shown that in 1960-61 there was appropriated in the vote for the defence research board the amount of $31,080,000 and that they expended $30,863,000.
May I have those figures given again?
Have you not a copy of this document? This is the national defence blue book which was issued several months ago.
Oh, yes. I was wondering whether that information is taken from the public accounts figures. Is that taken from the public accounts figures?

No. The public accounts for this fiscal year about which we are talking-
I refer to 1960-61-are not out yet.
I know that. That is why I could not get them; but would the figures be the same?
Yes; I think they would be approximately the same.
There is just one point I wish to make. The minister has stated that there has been a steady increase in research and development-*
No; not development.
All right; we will take it as being for research. He mentioned that in 1951 we were spending $23 million on research. In 1959-60 the total expenditure as given in the public accounts was $39,183,481.
I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but once more he has research and development lumped together.

I know that. I would ask the minister to allow me to finish. That is the total expenditure. If the minister will be patient for a minute or two I will explain what I mean. I am saying that of that amount of $39 million, roughly $11.5 million was spent on development which leaves approximately $27.5 million for research. Hence from 1951 up to 1960, we have gone up only from $23 million to approximately $27 million. I still maintain that is not a sufficient rate of increase for this important work. I think we should be spending two or three times as much as that having regard to the changing circumstances, the deterioration of the world situation and the increased emphasis on mechanical and technical research and development.

If the hon. gentleman will get this publication, if he has not already obtained it, and if he will consult it, he will see what the expenditures were each year from 1952-53 up to the present time. The actual expenditure for 1959-60 was $27,696,000 as far as research was concerned. The chief scientist on the board here just informs me that they have never yet been able to spend the whole amount of money appropriated because of the difficulty of getting the proper kind of people to carry on this experimental work. They are difficult to procure and there is always a shortage of them.
Supply-National Defence
You have to pay them.
I appreciate the minister's position and I thank him for his explanation. However, I hope he will see my point. My point is that the $27 million that we spent last year-
No; $30 million.

-or in 1959-60, will only have the same dollar value or same dollar equivalent as the $23 million we spent in 1951 because the dollar has gone down in value by 2 per cent a year since then. That is just about 20 per cent. If you take 20 per cent off the figure of $27 million you are back to about the same figure as 1951. I think what we have been doing is keeping pace with the depreciation of the Canadian dollar.

Just before this vote carries, Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few remarks. I may be using the words "research" in a broad fashion, but I feel it would be advisable at this time for some research and re-assessment to be carried out with regard to the location of our major airports in British Columbia.
At the present time our major military installations in British Columbia are pretty well grouped along the coast. I should like to enter a plea to the minister to have some research carried out on the selection of sites in the interior of British Columbia. In the event that the airports or installations are wiped out on the coast, the next installations are apparently in Alberta, located at Calgary and Edmonton. There are several ideal locations in the interior of the province which are suitable for development and research.

Mutual aid-
244. Contributions to infrastructure and military costs of the North Atlantic treaty organization and the transfer of defence equipment and supplies and the provision of services and facilities for defence purposes in accordance with section 3 of The Defence Appropriation Act, 1950, not exceeding a total of $40,798,000 including the present value of defence equipment or supplies or the cost of services made available by the Canadian forces estimated in the amount of $24,848,000 and provided by appropriations for those forces in the current and former years in respect of which, notwithstanding subsection (3) of section 3 of the said act, no amount shall be charged to this appropriation or paid into a special account; provided by this vote, $15,950,000.

Mr. Chairman, I thought it would be interesting to look back over the years not only with respect to expenditures on research and development but also on mutual aid. I wish to place on the record some figures I have taken from the public accounts and use them as a basis for some questions I should like to put to the minister later.
It was not easy to obtain these figures because we did not call it mutual aid in the beginning. The first time there was any allocation for this purpose was in 1951. That was tied up with the allocation for pensions, and the figure was around $144.5 million. In 1952 we allocated $235 million for special aid. Then $289.7 million in 1953 for NATO, and in 1954 we got around to calling it mutual aid.
In 1954 we allocated $253.4 million; in 1955 the figure was $175 million; in 1956, $133.5 million; in 1957, $118.5 million; in 1958 there was a drop down to $13.4 million, and in 1959 the expenditure was $18.4 million. These figures, again, have been taken from the public accounts of those years.
Last year in the estimates we allocated $14.8 million and this year we have before us another item of $15.9 million. Looking back over these figures we see there was a steady decrease from $235 million in 1952 down to $118 million in 1957. But in 1958 there was a very sharp decrease, from $118 million down to $13 million, and it has been around that average for every year since, with the exception of 1959, when the figure was around $18 million.
So for the last four years, 1958 to 1961, inclusive the figures only add up to about $62 million, which is a little less than half of the amount we spent in 1957. If we add all these figures together they total around $1.4 billion.
While I realize that the bulk of it has been spent on stock, equipment, parts and so forth, it does promote two questions in my mind. First, what has been the result of this contribution on the part of Canada over the past ten years? Second, on what basis have
[The Deputy Chairman.]

these figures been arrived at? Have these contributions been evaluated on the actual cost of the equipment we contributed, on the replacement cost or the depreciated cost, because I presume some of it was used. I do not expect the minister to give me the figures for the whole period, but I wonder whether he could tell the committee how much of this money, if any, was contributed in cash.
When we look at the sharp drop from $118 million in 1957 to $15 million or $16 million this year, the other question which comes to our minds is, what is the future of this mutual aid? Is it something that is going to be wound up and will disappear in the near future, or are there continuing commitments which will require a vote for a considerable time in the future?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member mentioned the purpose of this vote, which was to build up the strength of our NATO partners in Europe. This is why there is a period when the expenditures under this item were quite heavy, since when they have gradually been cut down.
Once again looking at this comparison of expenditures by fiscal years in the blue book, as far as aircrew training is concerned, for example, the amount went from $104 million down to $71 million, $52 million, $51 million, $47 million, $26 million, $6 million, and then nothing. That is because during those years 1952 to 1958-59 we were carrying on the training of a considerable number of airmen from the various NATO countries of Europe. That phase is now over so those expenditures are no longer being made.
During the same period we were supplying a large amount of equipment to these people to build up their stocks. That phase of the program is over to a great extent. Where you see this big drop in 1958-59 of $70.7 million to $18.3 million in 1959-60, the $18.3 million figure represents all cash contributions, whereas from there over it was some cash but mostly equipment taken out of stocks, and so forth.
The hon. member wanted to know how these figures were arrived at. As far as new equipment given as mutual aid is concerned, the actual cost of it is the figure used. So far as used equipment is concerned, or equipment which has been in stock for a considerable time, it was the estimated present value which was used in most cases. In some cases the replacement cost was used. It would depend on the type of item it was and whether it was an item which would be replaced or not. As to the question whether this is coming to an end, the answer is, no. Actually, the $50 million which is being appropriated to

supply F-104's to the NATO countries is a further contribution on our part toward mutual aid.
Could the minister tell the committee what material, if any, is being supplied to Portugal under this vote?
There is none being sent to Portugal at the present time.

National defence general-
245, To authorize, notwithstanding section 30 of the Financial Administration Act, and subject to allotment by the treasury board, total commitments of $2,674,046,619 for the purposes of the foregoing votes relating to national defence, regardless of the year in which such commitments will come in course of payment (of which it is estimated that $1,123,561,879 will come due for payment in future years), $1.

This item is probably one of the most important in the whole of the estimates of the Department of National Defence because it authorizes the government to make defence commitments in respect to procurement outlined in the book of estimates. It is the item which sets the course, the item which sets the direction for the future. It is the item which, to a very large degree, controls the flexibility of future expenditure. It governs to a large extent the course of Canadian defence policy for years to come. As a consequence, I cannot let this item pass without going back to some of the cardinal issues which face us. These are: how can Canada best contribute to collective defence, and how can Canada best contribute to the preservation of peace. These are the issues. These are the questions which have to be asked, and these are the questions which have to be answered. The answers, of course, are not easy. The answers are profoundly difficult and there is considerable difference of opinion with respect to them.
Are atomic weapons necessary as part of Canada's contribution? That is a question on which there is certainly no unanimity. The Globe and Mail in what I consider to be a most thoughtful editorial dated September 14, 1961 entitled "The Nuclear Dilemma" breaks this fundamental question into its two logical parts: (1) Is it or is it not our duty to our allies to equip ourselves with atomic weapons in order to provide the best possible defence in our sector against attacks on SACEUR and (2) Do our obligations to NATO require us to go the whole way and accept warheads.
With regard to the former we have attempted to demonstrate that the measures now contemplated by the government make no significant contribution to the protection of SAC and make no significant contribution to the deterrent. The deterrent would be as strong without these measures as it would
Supply-National Defence be with them. It is our opinion therefore, as we have indicated during this debate, that it is not necessary to have two Bomarc squadrons nor is it necessary to arm our defence squadrons with nuclear warheads. This is a new situation. This, as we have said, was not true in the past but it is true now and it will be true in the future. In the past an effective defence against the bomber did, in fact, help to protect SAC, but in the missile age this situation no longer exists and the experience of the past has to be reassessed.
Our problem in Canada is complicated by the fact that we have limited resources. The way in which these resources could best be utilized depends to a large extent on the point of view of the man with whom you are talking. If you were talking to the commander in chief of NORAD you would find that he naturally takes the position that Canada's main burden of effort should be in respect to the air defence of the North American continent. If you were talking to the commander in chief of the Atlantic forces you would find he would think it advisable for Canada to increase her contribution to the naval forces in the Atlantic. Of course, if you talk to the commander in chief of the Atlantic and ask him who is responsible for air defence against missiles he would say "talk to the commander in chief, NORAD" and if you asked the commander in chief NORAD he would tell you that you had better talk to SACLANT. Similarly, if you talked to SACEUR no doubt you would be told that building up our strength as part of the NATO shield was the most important thing on the priority list. This situation is not unusual. Each service grudgingly admits a limited role for the others but emphasises that it has the essential role and must have the larger share of the total budget. Melding these widely diverse opinions, each put forward in good faith by sincere and competent officers is a difficult task. They cannot all be right.
The minister takes pride in the acquisition of the Bomarc and the Voodoo, alleging that they will make a significant contribution to defence. Well, an old pal of his whom he used to quote often in debates, disagrees with him. Major General W. H. S. Macklin, C.B.E. in an article entitled "What air power do we need?" has this to say:
Why, for instance, should not some of these squadrons be equipped with our own CL-44 transport which the Americans rejected? The 32 CL-44s that the government proposed to trade for Voodoos would contribute far more to the common defence of the western alliance than the Voodoos ever will.
We need other types of flexible air transport, too; planes that can operate without great concrete airfields, such as the famous Beaver, Otter, Caribou series, all made in Canada, and various types of load-lifting helicopter. It could never

Supply-National Defence
be argued that these sorts of aircraft will become obsolete as fast as they are issued. Good models last a long, long time.
There is, for instance, the reliable, if slow DC-3 still in use after over 20 years, and the North Star, which has been on the air force inventory, since 1947 or '48.
Lastly, we ought to have some aircraft that could intervene tactically in a land battle, without resort to the nuclear bombs that the Starflghter we are buying will need to be useful. We have had the R.C.A.F. for 37 years, but it is an astounding fact that never has our air force been able to act in battle with the Canadian army. The army got its air support in the second world war from the British and in Korea, from the United States.
What we require, in short, is an air force that can co-operate effectively with the other Canadian armed forces to carry out strategic decisions made in Ottawa.
Consider that for a dozen years we have trained and maintained a parachute force at staggering expense. But never, no, never, has the air force been able to lift it with its armament. Does this make sense?
We know neither the day nor the hour when some new crisis, like Korea, Suez, or Congo, or worse, may arise in Africa, Asia or elsewhere. It is Premier Khrushchev's stated intention to promote such crises.
The Air Force ought to have the strategic, long-range air lift that could get an armed force to the danger area with speed, and then keep it there, with or without great airfields in the theatre. And if the peace-preserving role of such a force should fail and war ensue, the air force should be able to fight, under the conditions imposed by the enemy and geography. We can rarely make war as we might like to.
In regard to the second question, as to whether our obligations to NATO require us to go the whole way and accept warheads, the minister and the Leader of the Opposition agreed that subject to certain conditions, the answer to that question might be yes. The Leader of the Opposition reiterated the position of the Liberal party. The first priority is to build up the conventional strength, to give it flexibility, to give it the capacity to withstand an onslaught, at least long enough for the decision to use nuclear arms to be made at the proper level, which is the political level, and in this case by the NATO alliance. Then, he said that as a second line only to be used when conventional forces failed or when found inadequate to meet a situation, should it arise, atomic warheads might be used by separate units, preferably units which are held in reserve for such a contingency. This is a point on which there is not too much disagreement between the Leader of the Opposition and the minister.
The minister's friend of yesterday does not even think that NATO should have nuclear arms. Mr. John Gellner in an article entitled: "Needed: A Revision of NATO Policy" states, in part, as follows:
As long as the pretence is kept up that nuclear weapons can compensate for deficiencies in men and material, those member countries of NATO which have been inclined to shirk their military responsibilities, anyway, will not be persuaded that

they must at long last start to pull their weight. As long as the dubious doctrine that nuclear weapons can be used in limited wars is adhered to, NATO will not be able to gather the conventional forces which it needs to deal with the kind of emergency with which it may be faced. Above all, unless a military policy is laid down which will put the weight equitably on, and make sense to, all the allies, NATO will remain largely ineffective, militarily. In that case, the alliance itself will be meaningless.
But the government seems to have made a decision contrary to Mr. Gellner's; at least by its actions the government seems to have made the decision, but by its words we are left in doubt. Has the government made a secret decision in respect to the use of atomic warheads? One might speculate on that. Or is the government in fact spending hundreds of millions of dollars on weapons it might not arm? Is it again this afternoon under this item seeking authority to commit this country to the advance expenditure of further hundreds of millions of dollars on weapons that reach their full potential only when armed with nuclear warheads while at the same time having no intention to use them? This is the question which has to be answered: Are we going to or are we not?
In the meantime the government's indecision is causing considerable embarrassment and concern both at home and apparently in NATO. John Gellner in an article entitled "New Hope in the Alliance" has this to say:
There Is another impression which a visiting Canadian gets at the headquarters of NATO, and it is not encouraging: The standing of Canada in the alliance seems to be less than it used to be. From having been instrumental in the founding of NATO, and a main driving force in it for many years, Canada has receded into the background, particularly politically-we have become "consumers of information" as a leading NATO representative politely put it.
The reason for this is that the present Canadian government obviously sets less store by NATO than by the United Nations-and is in this respect at variance with virtually all other allies who consider NATO a much more useful instrument of international policy than the U.N. Hon. Howard Green's statements at the ministerial meeting last December, and to a lesser degree in Oslo last May, have certainly been interpreted in that way. Canadian indecision on whether or not to adopt nuclear weapons also does not enhance Canada's prestige. Their adoption would be considered a logical consequence of our acceptance of NATO strategy, and more specifically of the "strike" role (involving attack with nuclear weapons) for the Royal Canadian Air Force air division in Europe. Their rejection, even though belated, would probably be understood. But our fence-sitting, just as our apparently lessened interest in the Atlantic alliance, merely act as a dampener on the currently soaring spirit in NATO.
What is the Canadian position with respect to nuclear arms? We do not know. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate asked earlier this afternoon if there was in existence a draft agreement awaiting signature under

which Canada would be able to obtain nuclear warheads under joint control. The minister said he would not say whether there is or is not a draft agreement awaiting signature. If there was not one would guess that the minister would say so, but we are left to conclude that the document is in existence awaiting signature.

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member should not appear to be quoting me as having said anything in that vein. What I said to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was that I was not prepared to satisfy his curiosity on the subject.

It will be unfortunate if this item carries and this debate concludes without the committee and the country receiving a clear statement of the government's policy. It is not a satisfactory situation.
May I say that in my opinion our present method of dealing with the subject of defence is quite inadequate. Under the parliamentary system parliament is responsible for the voting of funds and it is this process in which we are engaged at the present time. And yet, we do not have adequate information. Parliament and the people are not given the facts. I am not alleging that this is completely new under the present government. It is probably traditional under our system but it is more important now. It is more urgent because the subject of defence is much more complicated. It has at last become a matter of survival, a matter of life and death, even on the North American continent. As I said, the information given to parliament and the public is inadequate.
At one time we used to receive a white paper which contained at least an outline of Canadian defence policy. The British issue a white paper which contains a thorough and exhaustive outline of the opinions of that government with respect to national defence. We used to have a similar paper here but now we have nothing. We now receive a blue book and I might say it is appropriately named because it would certainly make one blue to read its contents. It contains no information whatsoever in respect to defence policy. It merely, as it says, contains some information in respect to the roles and activities of the armed services and the defence research board.
Other important documents vital to the Canadian people are not made public. For example, the Graham report on civil defence was not disclosed either to the house or the Canadian people. We are led to wonder what it contained.
In addition, the government colours the information it gives to the committee and to the
90205-6-532
Supply-National Defence Canadian people. I suppose that is only natural. The government has a particular point of view, right or wrong, and it wishes to acquaint the public with it. The opposition, if it has a contrary point of view, also selects the available evidence to support its case. The difference is that the government has dozens and dozens of public relations men working full time faithfully and dutifully grinding out the truth as the boss sees it. That is quite natural too. As a matter of fact, I think that our expenditure in the Department of National Defence on public relations and public relations people is too great. I think it is too costly for the amount of benefit received by the Canadian people. I would recommend that treasury board have a look at it when the estimates for next year are being prepared.
At the same time the minister has deliberately tried to create the impression that the opposition is uninformed, and because the opposition is not at liberty to disclose its sources without losing them their contributions are not always given the consideration in the press and elsewhere that might be the case if the sources could be authenticated. Some better system must be found. I am aware of the traditional situation with respect to our parliamentary institutions but I think the time has come for a change. I think we waste too much time. We could accomplish a great deal more if we were to face the facts and make the necessary adjustment.
We must have some mechanics for making information available to the elected representatives of the people and I think that a good solution would be a small standing committee on defence. This committee would in no way attempt to usurp the functions of the Minister of National Defence but it would have briefings by serving officers. It would visit defence installations and see the hardware about which we are talking. It could meet in camera and be given classified information with respect to the Russian threat and our capacity to cope with it. It could study all aspects of defence, national survival and related subjects.
The result would be a small body of informed representatives of the people who would then be in a better position to help parliament and the public in a responsible examination of the public business. I have no doubt some criticism would be avoided, but I am sure the criticism that would be levelled would be better prepared and more authoritative. It would be much more difficult under those circumstances for either government or

Supply-National Defence opposition to colour their points of view appreciably without fear of immediate refutation by informed persons. The press and the public would know that spokesmen were or should be well informed.
The committee might issue a declassified record containing the maximum possible information to assist the public in appreciating better the complexities of the subject of defence and its many ramifications. I think that it would contribute to an improvement of the standard of debate. It should reduce irrelevancies and, most important of all, it should permit parliament to fulfil its function which is to give careful, thorough and responsible examination of the proposed expenditures of the executive branch. It would assist the public in assessing the issues, gauging the different policies if different ones are proposed and reaching conclusions. It would increase public confidence in the parliamentary system. In view of the gravity of the subject, which I think is appreciated by all of us on both sides of the house notwithstanding that sometimes in the heat of battle we do and say things which would not be appropriate under cooler circumstances, I think that under the circumstances I have outlined such a committee would assist us to do our job, to do it responsibly and to do it properly, which is the objective we have in mind. I therefore urge the government to give sympathetic consideration to this suggestion, and I know that in doing so it will have the support of parliament and the Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, during the course of the debate in the last several days I think I have dealt with practically all of the matters which have been revived in the remarks just made, and I do not think it would contribute anything to the debate for me to repeat the arguments I have made throughout that period. I agree with the hon. member that too much time is wasted and has been wasted in this committee, most of it, I am sorry to say, by endless repetition of the same arguments in connection with the same subjects.
As far as committees are concerned, during the period from 1952 to 1957 there was, I believe, one committee during that time which met during two sessions of parliament. From 1957 to date there have been two separate committees which have dealt with defence matters. The hon. member is now advocating a standing committee on defence. This is something that certainly can be given consideration. Whether we should have a standing committee on defence as suggested or whether we should continue the system

which has been followed in the past of having special committees from time to time as conditions seem to warrant is really a matter for decision, and I have nothing definite that I can say on that at the moment.

speechtext: We will now proceed to the consideration of the estimates of the Department of Defence Production.
67. Departmental administration, $9,574,385. (Translation):

Mr. Chairman, in my statement today I would like to discuss the principal responsibilities and accomplishments of the Department of Defence Production and in this connection to follow the procedure that I have followed in the past, that is, of dealing, where possible with the votes in the order that they appear in our departmental estimates.
In the course of my statement I would like to give you a brief outline of the work of the Department of Defence Production. I would also like to refer to those instances where there are differences between the amounts which we are asking to be voted this year and those amounts which were voted last year.
Under the provisions of the Defence Production Act, my department has exclusive authority to procure the goods and services that are required by the Department of National Defence. As the funds required in connection with this primary responsibility of my department are provided by the Department of National Defence, the defence production estimates do not provide too clear an illustration of the level and nature of departmental activities. I referred to this aspect during the discussion of the estimates of my department last year. However, I think it is worth while to touch upon the point again at the very outset of this statement.

The responsibility for procuring the equipment and material required for the Department of National Defence has been the primary task of my department since its establishment in 1951. This responsibility is still of primary importance but there are today other responsibilities which are of ever increasing significance.
The growing complexity of new weapon systems illustrates in most vivid terms how difficult it is for Canada to undertake the development and production of such systems on a purely independent basis. Against this background of changing conditions I shall continue, as I have in the past, to look to the resources of Canadian industry, whenever possible, to produce the weapons and material required for our armed forces and, as in the past, I shall continue to examine the demands of the services to see how they can contribute to the creation of new skills and facilities in Canadian industry. I wish to make it clear, however, that in addition to these activities new ways must be found-and are being found-to not only maintain but extend the capabilities of our defence industry. In this regard I would like to point out that my department has the responsibility for promoting the sale of Canadian defence items to the United States and our other NATO allies as well as the responsibility for co-ordinating Canada's activities in connection with the efforts of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization to increase co-operation in research, development and production in order to attain maximum efficiency in standardization and production by member countries.
My department is also placing increased emphasis on activities in the field of industrial research and development. This step is necessary if we are to ensure that Canadian industry will succeed both in finding and exploiting opportunities in the field of production sharing as well as responding to the future requirements of our own services. I am firm in my intent that we should do our full part to make these efforts succeed. (Text):
In the field covered by aircraft procurement the main production program is the CF-104 and the associated J-79 engine. Production schedules are being met for this 200 aircraft program and already five aircraft have been allocated to an advanced flight test program. The similarity between the Canadian version of the F-104 aircraft and that adopted by certain other NATO countries -Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and Italy has resulted in close co-operation between the countries concerned. An officer of my department has been transferred to Germany as a representative to the European 90205-6-532J
Supply-Defence Production organization for direction and control of the F-104G program which is now a subsidiary body of NATO.
Defence production in Canada on behalf of the North Atlantic alliance is showing a marked increase with the order for 61 Caribou aircraft received by de Havilland from the United States army. Present negotiations contemplate an additional order for 53 aircraft. Other programs include the CC-106 and CL-44D, long range transports, Otter and Beaver aircraft. Contracts have also been placed for 3 UH-QE light observation helicopters for the R.C.A.F. and 21 for the Canadian army. These 24 light observation helicopters are being purchased from the Hiller Aircraft Corporation. Two Vertol model 107-11 heavy helicopters have been purchased from the Vertol division of Boeing of Canada Limited for the R.C.A.F. and the purchase of an additional four is being negotiated. Both these companies have placed business with Canadian contractors on a reciprocal basis in accordance with current production sharing policies and both are using the services of a significant number of Canadian subcontractors.
As a result of the phasing out of older types of aircraft, it is expected that there may be some reduction in the workload of repair and overhaul contractors. The new aircraft which are being introduced will offset to some extent the effects of this phase out but generally speaking the introduction will not have an effect this year.
Other factors such as decreased R.C.A.F. flying hours, reduced contractual expenditures, rising costs and reducing manhours are all tending to create a constantly diminishing workload in terms of manhours of employment for aircraft repair and overhaul contractors.
My colleague, the Minister of National Defence, announced to the house on September 11 that the CL-41A will be used as a basic jet trainer by the R.C.A.F.
My department, in co-operation with the Department of National Defence, is now working on detailed specifications for this aircraft, and we expect to request proposals from the various companies concerned within the next two or three weeks.
I also intend to enter into discussions with Canadair Limited with a view to assisting that company in the development of a systems trainer version of the CL-41A to be designated the CL-41R. This engineering study is primarily directed towards potential requirements by the NATO countries operating high performance jet aircraft with sophisticated navigation and radar systems.
The CL-41R would be used as an advanced systems trainer, in order to give the pilots complete systems training.
