The procurement and production of electronic equipment will continue at a high level. In airborne electronics, the major programs are related to the supply of fire control, communication, navigation, and identification systems for the CF-104 and the F-104G aircraft. There are also continuing retrofit programs for doppler navigation, communication and anti-submarine detection. Electronic training aids are increasing in importance, and flight and tactics simulators are being built for the R.C.A.F. and for the German, Netherlands and Belgian governments. There are other promising possibilities in foreign sales of this tactical simulator.
Communication equipment will be procured for the army including the requirements for national survival warning networks. Field radar and radiation detection equipment will also be obtained for the army. Programs for the Royal Canadian Navy include shipborne radar, navigation, identification and counter-measures equipment, and a new Canadian designed sonar. This sonar equipment is also being manufactured in Canada for the account of the Royal Navy and Royal Australian Navy.
Installation of the R.C.A.F. air defence communication system will continue and a major program to lease communications for the North American air defence system is underway. Operation and maintenance of the existing defence warning systems will also continue and ground navigation stations for air defence installations will be procured. Up-dating of equipment at existing air defence sites is in process and new stations will be installed.
Last October, the functions of the ammunition and gun branches of my department were combined to form the new armament branch which is now responsible for the procurement and production of all types of ammunition, explosive stores and weapons systems including fire control equipment, underwater weapons, guns, mortars, launchers and both guided and ballistic missiles.
In production at present to meet Canadian military requirements are small arms, torpedoes, antisubmarine mortars and projectiles, automatic rifles and naval destroyer-escort guns. In addition, a range of fire control instruments and a tank navigation system are being produced in Canada to meet U.K. and foreign as well as Canadian military requirements.
The shipbuilding program is continuing with particular emphasis, as during the past year, on the construction of six destroyer escorts of the repeat-Restigouche class. All contracts for the construction of these ships


were placed in Canadian shipyards. In addition, a very large number of components for these vessels are being purchased and manufactured in Canada.
Modernization programs are being initiated for the destroyer escorts of the St. Laurent class and also for the H.M.C.S. Crusader.
In addition to the destroyer escort program shipbuilding activities include the construction of the naval tanker supply vessel. A contract for this vessel was placed as a result of competitive tenders. This is the first time that a contract has been awarded for a large and complex Canadian naval vessel in this manner. A contract has also been placed as a result of competitive tenders for the construction of a hydrographic and oceanographic survey vessel for the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.
Ship repair work will, of course, expand with the increase in the size and complexity of the Canadian fleet. Contracts for repair work as well as those for construction and modernization provide considerable employment in our Canadian shipbuilding industry.
I would also like to refer briefly to the general purchasing program which covers those supplies and services which do not normally involve special production arrangements. These items are procured both through departmental headquarters and the 14 district purchasing offices of my department which are located across Canada from St. John's, Newfoundland, to Victoria, British Columbia. These requirements although usually individually small in dollar value represent a great variety of items and a large sum of money in total. It is anticipated that procurement of this type will be approximately the same as last year.
All the programs to which I have just referred have a bearing on the amount of vote 67. The defence production and development sharing responsibilities, which I shall discuss very shortly, also have a bearing on this amount.
As you will note, there is an increase of $911,549 under vote 67 as compared with the estimate for 1960-61. The largest individual item involved in this increase is the provision for salaries which has been increased by over $830,000. This, of course, reflects the adjustments in the salaries of the public service that were made last year.
Vote 68 covers the care, maintenance and custody of stand-by defence plants, buildings, machine tools and production tooling. The amount provided in this year's estimates, namely $888,700, represents an increase of $98,645 over the amount provided in the estimates for 1960-61. The provision is dependent upon decisions to be taken during

the fiscal year as to whether continued production stand-by arrangements or disposal action will be required. Accordingly, these requirements cannot be forecast in precise terms at this time.
Vote 69 and supplementary vote 507 provide for capital assistance to Canadian industry and also for the provision of assistance in connection with tooling and preproduction costs involved in bids submitted by Canadian industry under the Canada-United States development and production sharing program. This is another case where there is an element of contingency involved and, as you will appreciate, it was not possible at the time of the preparation of these estimates to anticipate the number of cases where Canadian firms will ask for assistance nor the degree of success that will be obtained in such bids. I shall discuss the provisions of this vote at greater length when I review the provisions of vote 72.
Vote 70 provides for the payment of grants to municipalities in lieu of taxes on crown-owned defence plants operated by private contractors. As I explained at the time of the consideration of last year's estimates these plants are ones that have been acquired by the crown under capital assistance programs of past years. The grants are computed on the normal assessment evaluation by the municipality concerned subject to adjustment with respect to services rendered. There is a very small increase in the amount that is being provided this year.
Vote 71 covers the provision of funds to establish qualified sources for component parts and materials. This vote was established in October 1958 in order to establish qualified component production sources essential to the production of military electronic equipment in Canada.
The object of this vote is to prepare Canadian companies to participate in the production of components for future Canadian military requirements, in order that it will be possible to increase the Canadian content of defence procurement in Canada. This, of course, has the added advantage of increasing the Canadian content in allied countries' requirements for similar items.
From October 1958, to August 31, 1961, more than $860,000 has been spent. Twenty eight contracts have been placed and 12 of these have been completed. In addition, 18 projects are under consideration. These cover a wide range of items, from basic ceramic and precision bearing facilities to transistors, fuel pumps and servo-synchro components.
The operation of this vote shows clearly that Canadian industry is capable of producing new military components to acceptable standards. Some form of government support is
Supply-Defence Production required in this area where advanced military technology is a necessity, and vote 71 includes the provision for $607,000 with an additional future year's commitment authority for $300,000.
Vote 72 and the portion of vote 69 dealing with tooling and preproduction costs concern the Canada-United States defence production sharing program, and I should like to discuss the progress of the program, and in particular, the development sharing aspects of that program at this time. I should also like to refer to the important efforts being made to expand the role of Canadian military equipment in the programs of our NATO allies.
During 1960 co-operation between Canada and the United States resulted in the broadening of the areas of opportunity for Canadian defence industry to compete for U.S. defence requirements as well as the streamlining of the procedures involved in such cases. Extensive efforts on both sides of the border were required in this regard. The result has been the elimination of most of the obstacles to Canadian industrial access to the U.S. defence market. For example, the Buy American Act and U.S. duty barriers have been eliminated for a broad range of defence supplies from Canadian industry. It is also important to note that the U.S. defence directives which were issued in late 1960 in connection with the return of offshore procurement to U.S. sources, do not apply to the procurement of Canadian supplies which are included in the defence production sharing program.
One form of financial assistance which is made available by my department to Canadian industry actively interested in sales to the United States is the sharing with Canadian companies of certain preproduction engineering and special tooling costs to enable Canadian companies to cope on more equal terms with competing firms which have been able to write off such costs against previous orders.
In 1959-60 $1,250,000 was voted for this purpose and the same amount was voted last year. As a result of firm commitments for this type of assistance totalling approximately $2.5 million about $20.1 million in production contracts had been received by Canadian companies by August 31, 1961. In addition, these companies have been placed in a position to compete for follow-on orders for similar supplies. Actual expenditures made against the votes for the past two fiscal years have totalled $1,230,554. In the current fiscal year $175,602 has been spent to the end of August.

Supply-Defence Production
Expenditures have been less than provided by the votes because oi the difficulties involved in attempting to forecast expenditures in this area. The production sharing program is a comparatively new responsibility and there has not been an opportunity to accumulate sufficient data to establish trends in expenditure. Second, it is not possible to anticipate the number of cases in which Canadian firms will seek support from these funds. Third, the number of competitive contracts that will be won by Canadian firms cannot be forecast, and of course, expenditures are only made when a Canadian company has received a contract. Finally, the rate of our expenditure depends upon the period of time covered by the contract and the receipt of billings for progress payments. For these reasons provisional commitments against this vote fluctuate greatly throughout the year and actual expenditures do not fully indicate the amount of support offered during the year. In order to continue this assistance in the establishment of production capacity there has again been included the sum of $1,250,000 under vote 69, and an additional $500,000 has been requested under the supplementary vote 507.
The other major type of assistance made by my department is our contribution to development sharing to encourage Canadian defence industry to maintain technological developments at a level which will promote future defence exports. The sum of $5 millions was approved in both 1959-60 and 196061 for this purpose. Expenditures for these two fiscal years amounted to $4,752,775. In the current fiscal year expenditures to the end of August totalled $706,185.
The difficulties involved in forecasting expenditures under vote 69 also apply in the case of this vote. In addition there is a further element which has prevented the full use of the funds that have already been approved. Research and development is by its nature a long process. Most programs require only modest funds in the initial study stages and large expenditures do not occur until prototypes, testing facilities, and such items are required. Some of our programs will be moving into this stage this year.
We are assisting development in such selected fields of United States defence interest as, for example radar and communications, V/STOL aircraft and turbine engines, antisubmarine warfare devices, plasma physics and surface transportation such as hydrofoil vessels and light weight high mobility vehicles.
This support of Canadian industry takes several complementary approaches to defence development sharing with the United States. We have ratified procedural arrangements

with the United States army and are now negotiating with the United States air force to the end that selected United States developments requirements will be undertaken in and financed by Canada. Furthermore, in support of uniquely Canadian projects whose successful development wiE be of interest to the United States services my department has placed contracts with competent Canadian companies. In addition, to equalize the position of Canadian industry in competition with United States industry for U.S. financed development requirements, we are arranging to share the cost of selected projects with the United States government and the Canadian companies concerned.
These activities to August 31 have resulted in the Canadian government's contribution of about $20.1 millions to development projects now awarded to Canadian companies or fully approved and pending only final contractual details. In addition to these firm commitments, there are a number of projects under active consideration including several unique Canadian concepts and formal U.S. requirements approved in principle for support. These amount to about $4.6 millions.
In addition to these projects, which total some $24.7 millions for Canadian expenditure on defence development projects in Canadian industry, a variety of development possibilities are under preliminary investigation. These figures, which do not include some $13.7 millions of U.S. funded research and development and technical engineering assistance contracts, or Canadian industry's own contributions, indicate that substantial U.S. oriented research and development is now taking place in Canadian defence industry.
Examples of major projects included in this Canadian development program are V/STOL aircraft, Avro, Canadair and de Havilland; turbine engines, Orenda and Pratt and Whitney; airborne electronic equipment, Marconi and Computing Devices; radar items, Long Sault Woodcraft and Fleet Manufacturing; communications equipment, Radio Engineering Products; and rocket vehicles, Bristol and Canadair.
In order to continue this work of sustaining technological capability in Canadian defence industry the sum of $5.5 millions with additional commitment authority for $11 millions has been included under vote 72. If this development sharing activity is as successful as the present trend indicates then I expect that supplementary estimates will be proposed before the end of this fiscal year.
As a result of our continued co-operative arrangements with the United States. I am now able to report an increasing flow in the number of United States defence development

and production sharing contracts awarded to Canadian industry. These contracts totalled $112.7 millions in the calendar year 1960.
This total includes $61 millions in United States government prime contracts with Canadian companies and $51.7 millions in United States industry subcontracts to Canada. It should be noted that such subcontracting was negligible before 1959 and is largely the result of our production sharing program. The 1959 and 1960 two year total for United States defence production sharing in Canada is $209 millions.
The first eight months of 1961 have shown a similar favourable trend. Production sharing contracts in this period involve some $79.9 millions made up of prime contracts for about $43 millions and subcontracts for about $36.9 millions. This compares with the total of $65 millions of such United States defence business placed in Canada in the first eight months of 1960. Some major items involved in the prime contract area were in connection with de Havilland Caribou aircraft and spares for various de Havilland aircraft, $7.7 millions; Pratt and Whitney Aircraft engine spares, repair and overhaul, $11.7 millions; Sparton sonobuoys, $1.1 million; Canadian Arsenals' cartridges, $3.9 millions; Radio Engineering Products field telephones, $1.6 million; Orenda engine development, $913,000; and Marsland Engineering, plotting tables, $2.6 millions. A firm order for Marconi airborne doppler navigation radar in the amount of $370,000 has been received and negotiations are under way to increase this to $1.7 million. There are good prospects for additional large orders.
Some of the subcontracts consisted of counter-measure systems, $1.2 million, to Northern Electric; switchboards for FPS-26, $830,000, to Federal Pacific; radar equipment, $2.3 millions, to Canadian Westinghouse; NA-SARR subsystems to Westinghouse, $3.5 millions: training and installation AN/FST=2B (SAGE) Burroughs, $1 million; missile components, $2.7 millions, to Sperry; and Bomarc parts and components, $1.3 million, to several Canadian companies.
Significant impetus has been given to the Canada-United States defence production sharing program by the F101-F104-Pine Tree agreement between the two governments announced by the Prime Minister on June 12. This agreement clearly indicates the sincere intent of the United States and Canadian governments to make defence production sharing a vital program. It will make a singificant contribution to maintaining Canada's defence production base. Many of our most important defence contractors will receive contracts and subcontracts.
Supply-Defence Production
Only governments can negotiate transactions of the magnitude of the one that I have just mentioned. Generally, however, the government's role lies in the creation of a climate of opportunity for Canadian industry to compete for United States defence business. Therefore, real success of the program is dependent upon the efforts of Canadian industry. In this regard some companies have shown commendable initiative and effort but unfortunately some others have been reluctant to accept the challenge. In order to further stimulate Canadian industrial activity in the production sharing program I again wrote on May 29 to the senior officers of Canadian firms which have indicated an interest in the program, outlining progress for the past year, the continuing need for co-operation from industry, and the opportunities available. I once again urge all companies with capability and resources to make a determined effort to gain United States defence business for Canadian industry.
I should now like to turn to another area, quite separate from production sharing, in which my department has been endeavouring to expand the role of Canadian developed defence equipment-I refer to our efforts to co-operate with our NATO allies in the research, development and production of defence equipment requirements.
By direction of the NATO defence ministers, the NATO armaments committee and its various sub groups are providing a means by which research, development and production requirements can be co-ordinated to the mutual advantage of all countries participating. My department is working closely with the Department of National Defence and others in this long range plan of NATO cooperation which will, I trust, ensure that Canadian capabilities are recognized in the light of NATO requirements. It should be emphasized that the purpose of this co-operation is co-ordination and not sales promotion, and it is in this spirit that we are participating.
We have found, however, that our increased efforts in the NATO area have had supplementary benefits. Several countries have placed contracts for current Canadian equipment. These contracts involve substantial benefits for Canadian companies.
The interest shown by certain of our NATO allies in our aircraft, radar, anti-submarine warfare equipment, navigational aids and other equipments developed by Canada is heartening. Every effort is being made by my department in close co-operation with the Department of National Defence and Canadian industry to provide demonstrations, items for test purposes, and the administrative machinery to ensure that our industry is not in

Supply-Defence Production a disadvantageous position in relation to other potential suppliers in the European area.
We intend to provide financial support for preproduction and tooling costs and development costs, similar to that we now provide to companies entering the United States defence market. Support of a company under the production sharing program has a secondary benefit in that it also assists the same company in its efforts to sell to our overseas allies.
With respect to administrative machinery, I have offered to the defence ministers of our allies, the services of the Canadian Commercial Corporation to act on behalf of their governments and prime contractors in the procurement of defence equipment and supplies in Canada. Use of this crown corporation ensures that any purchases made by a foreign government will be negotiated and administered by the Department of Defence Production employing the same procedures and safeguards as are followed by the department in procuring supplies for the Canadian services. Such assurances are valuable to both foreign governments and Canadian suppliers since they eliminate many of the difficulties inherent in the establishment of new commercial relationships over large distances and outside of traditional military procurement channels.
The benefits which may accrue to Canadian industry in the years ahead as a result of co-operation with our NATO allies are indicated by the successful sales of Canadian developed products in connection with the F-104 aircraft adopted by Canada and other NATO countries. In 1960 letters of intent authorizing the manufacture of flight simulators up to about $3.5 millions were received. The total probable procurement involves about $22 millions. These flight simulators are produced by Canadian Aviation Electronics Co. for sale to Germany and the Netherlands. Our expectations are that further orders from other countries for these equipments will be received.
In addition, as a result of our arrangements with Lockheed Aircraft Corporation, we have received orders worth approximately $15.5 million for the wings, rear fuselage and empennage of F-104 aircraft. Further such procurement from Canadian sources may result in substantial future orders.
Other Canadian equipment has also found a place on these aircraft and I refer specifically to the electronics equipment sold to Lockheed for inclusion in the F-104's that have been sold by that corporation to overseas governments. For example position and homing indicator systems produced by Computing Devices of Canada and sold to Lockheed for Germany involve a value of $2.1
[Mr. O'Hurley.l
million. I have, of course, already reported these Lockheed orders as U.S. production sharing subcontracts.
In our efforts in the European area we are not neglecting our traditional relationship with the United Kingdom. Two major sales of Canadian developed items to the United Kingdom in 1960 were the sale of de Havilland Beaver aircraft and also variable depth sonars produced by EMI-Cossor Electronics.
For the first eight months of 1961, some $2.5 million in actual prime contracts were placed through the Canadian Commercial Corporation alone, covering such diverse fields as flight and tactics trainers (Canadian Aviation Electronics) and variable depth sonars (EMI-Cossor). In addition de Havilland has received this year prime contracts direct from Ghana for Otter, Beaver and Caribou aircraft totalling about $8.4 million; Orenda Engines has received about $4.8 millions direct from West Germany for spares, and Jarry Hydraulics has received about $1 million direct from West Germany for power flight controls. Furthermore, Canadair has received this year about $1.3 million in subcontracts from German and Dutch prime contractors for components for the F-104, and Computing Devices received contracts for P.H.I. systems valued at approximately $8.3 million destined for Germany, France and Italy. Further orders for such equipment are expected from NATO countries and their prime contractors. In most cases these sales were part of major continuing programs placed in Canada as a result of technological skill, competitive pricing and active selling by Canadian industry with the assistance of government departments concerned. For the first eight months of 1961 the total overseas defence business reported by Canadian companies, including the above-mentioned contracts, amounted to $28.8 millions.
In all these activities my department is fortunate in that it has developed over the years the machinery and the specialized knowledge of production and procurement officers essential in the field of military procurement. This background now enables us expeditiously to promote Canadian capabilities to meet the defence requirements of allied countries wherever they may arise. The efforts required are most substantial, entailing, among other things, considerable liaison abroad. I should like to say that the members of my department are pursuing these matters with energy and dedication.
Our progress in our efforts to expand the use of Canadian defence equipment both by our overseas allies, and also by the United

States in our production sharing program has been encouraging. We shall continue these efforts in a most vigorous fashion.
Mr. Chairman, in light of the recent unfortunate change in the international situation, I wish to bring the house up to date on the planning for a war supplies agency that has been going forward in the emergency supply planning branch of the department since May of last year.
As I explained in presenting last year's estimates, and as the Prime Minister reiterated on September 13, the government has decided that should nuclear war break out a war supplies agency would be brought into existence immediately, by order in council under the War Measures Act, to assume responsibility for all aspects of control over the production, distribution and pricing of supplies for both civil and military purposes, with the exception of certain aspects of the agricultural and fishing industries.
An interim organizational structure for the war supplies agency, designed to meet the anticipated needs for the period immediately following nuclear attack, has been developed and approved. Within the over-all organization of the war supplies agency, there will be national, regional, zonal and local components, in conformity with the system of emergency government being developed by the emergency measures organization under the direction of the Prime Minister. The staffing of the national component of the war supplies agency has been completed by the selection on a stand-by basis of suitably qualified persons from various government departments and agencies in Ottawa. The staffing of the ten regional components, likewise on a stand-by basis, is near completion. I might add that the war supplies agency was fully represented at the national level during exercise TOCSIN 1961 and had a nucleus staff at each regional headquarters. In the further exercise to be held this fall the war supplies agency will participate fully at both national and regional levels.
In connection with the staffing of the regional components of the war supplies agency, hon. members might be interested to know that arrangements are being made with the various provincial governments to draw on their personnel resources as well as on the field staffs of various federal departments and agencies. Formal agreements to this end are currently being negotiated. The next step in the organization of what might be termed a "shadow" war supplies agency, will be the establishment of the appropriate components at the zonal and local levels. For this purpose we would expect to draw on the personnel resources of business and industry as well as on federal and provincial field staffs.
90205-6-533
Supply-Defence Production
One of the major tasks of the war supplies agency, should it ever have to be brought into existence, would be to assess the country's surviving material resources. To provide the basis for making such an assessment, the emergency supply planning branch has initiated a research program designed to produce in readily useable form comprehensive inventory data on major stocks of essential commodities and related production facilities normally available in the country. This research program is necessarily long term in character, but substantial results have already been achieved with respect to the collection and processing of data on stocks of food and petroleum products. Methods have been developed in co-operation with the army and emergency measures organization for evaluating surviving resources after attack.
A third major aspect of our planning has been the preparation in draft form of various regulations and orders likely to be required by the war supplies agency in exercising effective control of supplies under conditions of nuclear war. Among other things, a plan for the emergency rationing of essential consumer goods is now before the government.
The staff of the emergency supply planning branch remains small. There are at present 12 officers at headquarters in Ottawa and five regional officers. Two additional officers for the headquarters staff and four more regional officers are currently being recruited.

I should like to thank the minister for his very thorough and almost exhaustive report. He has gone over the activities of the department very carefully and he has given us considerable detail with respect to the projects on which it is presently engaged.
Last year we went over most of the items of this department very thoroughly and consequently it is not our intention to debate them at length on this occasion, particularly in view of the fact that a considerable portion of the money being asked for has already been spent.
There are, however, one or two questions which we shall ask on the details, and there is one I should like to ask at this time under the general subject of administration. The minister mentioned that although the amount of production sharing which had been obtained from the United States so far this year was greater than in the first eight months of last year it is, however, only about half last year's total. I wonder if the hon. gentleman could give the committee some assurance that during the remaining four months of the year the amount of business obtained will bring the total up well beyond last year's figure.
8442	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production
Last year in this committee there was some talk about contracts we hoped to get from Germany, Belgium and other European countries. Were we successful?

The discussion at the time was concerned with the simulator program and possible orders from Germany, Holland and Belgium. We obtained those contracts. We won the competition and we were awarded the contracts. The simulators are being built in Montreal at the present time for those countries, as well as to satisfy the Canadian order.
Could the minister indicate in round figures the total amount involved in those contracts?
As it stands today the figure is around $3 million, but the total contract is going to be worth more than $20 million.

My intention is to ask the minister a series of questions rather than to make specific comments. I placed some queries on the order paper before the summer recess and in due course I received some answers which are contained in sessional paper 267B of September 7. I should like to make some inquiries of the minister concerning the information contained in that sessional paper and the answers given to particular questions.
My inquiry had to do with subventions, or subsidies. The question which I asked was whether, since January 1, 1950, any subventions had been paid to any incorporated companies other than crown corporations and, if so, what was the amount of the subvention, the total amount paid to each company, and so on. Some of the information which was given to me by the Department of Defence Production contains the names of companies such as the Canadian Marconi Company, Canadian Steel Foundries, Canadian Steel Improvement, Canadian Vickers-a number of companies which have received subventions from the Department of Defence Production in respect of certain types of work. The information lists the fields of endeavour in which each of these particular companies are engaged-electronics, shipbuilding and the like for the period, I take it, from April 1, 1959 to May 31, 1961.


In so far as one part of the answer is concerned a total of about $1,250,000 is shown as having been paid to these companies by way of subvention or subsidy. I wonder if the minister could explain the reason for these particular subventions. I do not know whether the hon. gentleman has before him a copy of this particular sessional paper. If he has, it will not be necessary for me to go into detail with regard to the particular companies. However, if the minister has not got the list I could go into greater detail. Before doing so, I wonder if the minister is familiar with this particular subject matter I have before me.

I do not know whether this information would be sufficient but these subsidies or subventions are really payments in respect to pre-production and engineering assistance in connection with contracts for the United States. Would the hon. member for Skeena mind giving me a few examples? I have not got that paper before me today.

Certainly. For example, the first company mentioned on this list is Beaconing, Optical and Precision Materials, of Montreal, Quebec. They are engaged in the electronics business and they received a subvention during the period between April 1, 1960 and May 31, 1961, to a total amount of $23,000. The authority for payment is given as treasury board minute 573346 of December 12, 1960. The second entry deals with the same firm and the amount is $25,596 over the same period of time. I think that, perhaps, will be sufficient.

I have a copy here of the answer given to the hon. member for Skeena at the time. These subventions were approved by treasury board, by the Department of National Defence and by the Department of Defence Production, this, of course, being a joint venture. The amounts are for tooling and pre-production so as to be competitive in obtaining United States contracts.
This was in order that we might be competitive with United States firms?
In the United States market.
Does the same reason apply in respect to the subsidies paid to each of the companies listed? Was it a question of competition?
Yes, Mr. Chairman.

I wonder if I might ask a further question of the minister based on the same order. This is headed "Establishment of Qualified Production Sources of Components and Materials". I take it this relates to something different because in some instances the

same companies are listed-the Canadian Marconi Company and Canadian Arsenals, for example. This also applies to subventions given for some other reason. The total for the four year period is shown as $811,715. There is a further reply headed "Sustainment of Canadian Industrial Technological Capability". This is for a three year period and the total amount is $4,919 million.
Can the minister explain what is meant by the heading "Establishment of Production Sources of Components and Materials", the further heading "Sustainment of Canadian Industrial Technological Capability" and offer an explanation concerning the various subventions?

Mr. Chairman, the first question concerns vote No. 71. With a view to ensuring the maximum participation of Canadian firms in defence procurement, this requirement was first set up to establish qualified sources of supply of component parts and materials sufficiently in advance of Department of National Defence contract demands to lessen the dependence of end product producers on United States and other sources of supply. These are products we used to buy outside Canada which are now procured for the department in Canada. The program is essentially one of developing industrial capability in the military components field. It is to assist Canadian manufacturers to produce in Canada components to meet the requirements of the Canadian armed forces.
The hon. gentleman's other question related to vote No. 72. This vote was raised in 1959-60 to further the stated policy of the Canadian government of sustaining a research and development capability in Canadian industry with which to undertake the sharing of defence development and production tasks with the United States.
What is the future expectation with respect to engaging in subvention of this type? Will the activity diminish, increase or remain stable?

Over the next few years we expect an increase in this activity which is valuable in providing work for Canadian industry. For the assistance of the hon. member I should point out that this activity prepares Canadian industry by assisting it to acquire skills that were not previously available. The benefit applies to defence and civil industries. They are able to acquire skills which they lacked previously and can thus produce material we formerly had to purchase outside Canada.

I cannot resist commenting that I find it strange that these private enterprise companies should require assistance 90205-6-533J
Private Bills
through the government from the Canadian taxpayer. I am not complaining about our helping them from time to time in the development of Canadian industry to ensure that as much of this work as possible is done in Canada but these are rugged individualists who in this case are asking the Canadian taxpayer to take the risk for them.

Would the minister indicate to the committee what were the Canadian purchases for defence equipment in the United States for 1960 in relation to both contracts and subcontracts and what they have been this year to date?

The following are the Canadian government's defence purchases placed directly in the United States. In 1959, prime contracts $47 million; subcontracts $61.2 million. In 1960, prime contracts amounted to $83.3 million; subcontracts $113 million. For the first six months of 1961 the figures are as follows: prime contracts $18.7 million; subcontracts $36.4 million.
These figures do not include contracts for defence equipment placed by Canadian industry directly in the United States?

Yes, they do include those
contracts which related to defence purchases.
Item agreed to.

Mr. Chairman, now that the estimates of this department have been passed by the committee may I take this opportunity to extend my appreciation to hon. members of the committee. I think we have probably established a record for the passage of the estimates of this department. I wish to assure the committee of my continuing co-operation and understanding.

As long as the minister appreciates that this does not establish a precedent.

subtopic: AMENDMENT REQUIRING DISCLOSURE OF CAMPAIGN FUND CONTRIBUTIONS
AMENDMENT REQUIRING DISCLOSURE OF CAMPAIGN FUND CONTRIBUTIONS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-50, to amend the Canada Elections Act (election expenses).
He said: Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on second reading of this bill I might say that while technically we are dealing with the second reading, in actual fact we are really resuming debate on a bill that has been before the house for many years before I had the privilege of attending this chamber. It is very interesting also, and I think the house should be reminded of this, that such a bill has always been introduced by a member of this party. Similar bills have been introduced for many years by members of the C.C.F. party but unfortunately we have never had an expression of opinion of the house on the measure. The history of the bill in the past is that it has always been talked out, first by Liberal government members and then by Conservative government members. I should like to express the hope that after all these years we may have reached the stage where we can at least give second reading to the bill and accept the principle.
However, Mr. Speaker, the efforts of this group over many years have not been entirely lost because there is a growing interest and concern about this matter. We see examples of this right across the country from coast to coast. We are aware, and it has been referred to before, of the great assistance in

this regard that was rendered by two members of the clergy in the province of Quebec who, having become most concerned about corruption that arose out of contributions to political parties, proceeded to write a very thought-provoking article in this regard that has had great and beneficial results, particularly in the province of Quebec.
I should like to make it very clear that this problem is not confined to that province. It is very fine for those of us who come from other provinces to point a finger at Quebec and say that the problem is much worse there than in any other province but unfortunately that is not the case, as I intend to prove in my few brief remarks when I refer to certain articles that have been written.
It is our contention that a great deal of the corruption and a great deal of the fear and uneasiness that are growing across the country can certainly be curtailed, if not eliminated completely, by the adoption of a measure such as Bill No. C-50 which compels political parties to reveal the sources of their funds. I recall that some two years ago when a bill similar in many respects was being debated in the house a question was asked by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome). I believe the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) was speaking at the time. As found on page 2744 of Hansard for April 16, 1959, the hon. member for Vancouver South asked the following question:
When your party evolves into the party you expect it to be, will you still be introducing a bill concerning the disclosure of election expenses.
I do not think there is any better answer than the fact that today, after the event has come about which was referred to two years ago, we who are now within the confines of the New Democratic party are introducing a bill similar to the ones we introduced when we were in the C.C.F.
We have also heard various spokesmen from the other parties expound the theory that it might be better if members did not know from where their support came. I believe that the same hon. member for Vancouver South expressed this idea as found on page 5308 of Hansard of June 30, 1959. I think he missed the point. The important thing is not that the candidate or member should know the source of these funds. Rather, it is that the public should know the source of these funds and that the house assembled here should know their source. Hon. members should know if breweries, contractors, yes, trade unions, contribute their money to support any political party. The house should know so that these factors can be taken into consideration when members are considering legislation that comes before the house. When legislation which is of

particular benefit to an organization that has contributed substantially to the party in power at any particular time, comes before the house I think it would be a very useful thing for the house to be fully aware of what has taken place in the past.
I should like to refer to two articles in recent issues of Maclean's magazine which deal with the subject matter of the bill now before us. The first one, written by Mr. Peter Newman, is found in the issue of May 6, 1961, some few months ago. It is entitled, "Who'll Pay the Record Shot for Our Next Election?". The subheading is, "The Smart Contributors Buy 'Insurance' with the Two Old Parties". The first paragraph reads as follows:
No process in the working of Canadian democracy is surrounded by a climate of greater mystery than the collection of campaign funds by political parties. The innuendo of scandal is so strong that the details of party finances can seldom be traced beyond the whispered exaggerations of Ottawa gossip.
I think that is one mystery which, if it is going to remain, should be made an illegal offence. He goes on to express the danger, as he sees it, of the streamlining of what I would call this malpractice that has gone on for so many years in our country. He goes on to say:
The Conservatives have set a precedent by appointing to the cabinet a man believed to be specifically charged with financial matters.
Certainly if that statement is true, and I do not know whether it is, it gives rise to further concern. Mr. Newman goes on to mention the methods used and says:
The biggest donors, as in past elections, are expected to be the large corporations, indulging in what they call "necessary" giving. These are contributions made without any expectation of specific returns, beyond the preservation of free enterprise and the two party system. The donation is almost always split 60-40, with the party in power getting the bigger share.
The interesting thing about this suggestion is that it is verified in another article to which I should like to refer in a moment, an article written by no less a person than the former national organizer for the Liberal party. Mr. Newman goes on to deal with another group which he says is much more dangerous than the one he has already mentioned, and says:
The most willing contributors to party treasuries are some of the contractors who deal in government work. They usually make the gift to the party in power fairly openly, but quietly also take out some insurance by making a smaller donation to the opposition.
Then he concludes his article by referring to what is probably the greatest known scandal of this kind that has ever hit a federal government.
Private Bills
The last paragraph of this article reads as follows:
Meanwhile, the present system mysteriously continues to produce millions of dollars for the party war chests. Probably the most forthright clue came from R. O. Sweezey, the president of the Beauharnois Power Corporation, who in the late 1920's contributed about $700,000 to the Liberal party, after his company had secured hydro rights on the St, Lawrence. The contribution had been necessary, he said, because "gratefulness was always regarded as an important factor in dealing with democratic governments."
I think that outlines very clearly the situation. This problem has existed for many years in this country. In order to indicate that feeling of concern is growing, and growing at a very rapid rate, I should like to point out that not only was this article published in May of this year but we also find another one in a recent issue of Maclean's magazine. I should like to recommend this article to all hon. members. It was written by Mr. James Scott who, until recently, was the national organizer of the Liberal party. He says, "Political slush funds corrupt all parties".
There are some allegations or suppositions in this article of Mr. Scott's which I certainly cannot accept. For example, while he very frankly points out the contributions in the past and mentions specific cases, and after all as the national organizer of one of the two major parties in the country he should know what he is talking about in that respect, he goes on to say something to the effect that because the New Democratic party might have funds available to them in a somewhat unequal proportion to that of the other parties, the whole idea should be abolished.
I should like to submit that it is not in the giving of this money to political parties that the evil lies. I submit it is in the secretive giving. If any company wants to donate to the Liberal party or the Conservative party, it should be its privilege to do so. However, the public should be made aware of what it is doing. Then, the public could realize possibly why it is being done. As I say, it is very important when we have to deal with legislation in this house that we should be aware of any facts along this line. Mr. Scott endeavours to create the impression that it is just as evil for say a million members of the Canadian labour congress to contribute their 60 cents a year to the New Democratic party as it would be for one individual to contribute $600,000 a year to one of the other parties. I think any reasonable man would realize there is a great deal of difference here. Contribution of 60 cents a year from an individual would not place him in the same preferred position that a much larger contribution by an individual or by a company seeking favours from a government would be in as a result of that contribution.

Private Bills
Again, on page 67 of this issue of Maclean's for September 9, we find some very interesting point to which I should like to refer. As I say, both Mr. Newman and myself are in agreement as to what occurred in the past. I quote:
However, the biggest corporate donors for the most part do not attempt to intervene directly in party policy. Generally speaking, they contribute to both the Conservative and the Liberal parties. The traditional split is usually 60 per cent to the party in power and 40 per cent to the party in opposition, but this is subject to many variations.
He points out how widespread this practice is. On page 67 I also find this:
Nevertheless, nobody who holds office or hopes to hold office can ignore his benefactors. Any citizen of Canada can lay his views before the Prime Minister or the Leader of the Opposition but, human nature being what it is (and these men are human), a man whose firm donates $25,000 or $50,000 to a political party every election is likely to get through to the party leader a lot faster than somebody the party never heard of.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I say that the evil here is not in the giving. The evil is in the fact that nobody knows about it except the two parties involved; that is where the danger lies. Then, on page 69 of this article, I find this, and this is something to which I referred a little while ago when I said that the favourite pastime of every province was to point the accusing finger at the province of Quebec.
It is often assumed in the rest of Canada that this occurs only in the province of Quebec, but this is far from the truth.
A year or two ago, during a provincial election campaign in another province I received a call from a small contractor of my acquaintance. He told me he had been telephoned by an official of the government party of the province who instructed him to have $2,000 ready in cash by the following week. It would be picked up by a party legman and would be the contractor's contribution to the party's campaign funds. This man's entire business had been built up on government contracts and he asked me what to do. I told him to give the man the money and me an affidavit stating how and why he had made the contribution. We could have broken the whole thing wide open; my informant told me other contractors had received similar instructions. But they were all frightened. They all paid up and kept quiet about it.
It is not my intention to take up too much of this private members' hour in speaking on this subject. I think I have pointed out some of the dangers involved. I think I have pointed out the fact that this practice is widespread and has gone on for many years. I feel it is time this matter was given serious consideration because if this practice continues unabated it will undermine our whole democratic system. This bill, Mr. Speaker, is designed to eliminate this danger, and I hope it receives approval in principle in this house today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on this particular bill today I do not

need to go into any detailed complaining or crying as the hon. member who just resumed his seat has done. I am not exactly sure where he stands with regard to former C.C.F. policy and that of the New Democratic party. I should like to draw to the attention of the house the fact that he is in no position to try to bluff as he has done today. It is nothing short of a bluff when any member gets up in this house and tries to make a case based on facts derived from some national magazine, of which he has no personal knowledge and for which he is more or less dependent on someone else.
I say it is a bluff for the simple reason that the success of the former C.C.F. party- if it is a former party because that is yet to be decided in view of the fact there does not seem to be the collusion between the two parties that they would like to have-is directly related to its success in the field of collections. If I may put it another way, the success of his political party at the polls is directly related to its success in the field of collections. You can see for yourself why they get up and complain.
The hon. member has referred to the fact that it is the secrecy of the giving that is evil and dangerous. I think if the Canadian people were given a choice they would rather have secret giving than the intimidation which has been imposed upon the workers and trade union men of this country by this New Democratic party in extracting 60 cents a year from these individuals. I say "forced upon the workers of this country" for the simple reason that it is nothing less than that. They have evolved a system whereby 60 cents per capita be taken from the members of an affiliated union of the Canadian labour congress. If any one individual does not choose to pay this 60 cents, he is given this democratic right to contract out. How can any man in this house stand up and imply that he belongs to anything that is democratic when they collect 60 cents a head from every individual who belongs to an affiliated union of the Canadian labour congress? How can they refer to this procedure as democratic?

This hon. member has more experience than and just as much knowledge as the hon. member for Timmins who has just taken his seat as to what goes on in local

unions. I can give him and the other members of his party quite a rundown of how this develops. I might say that if he himself professes to be democratic, he will stand up and deny the attitude adopted by the new party in that they are giving every man an opportunity to contract out on this 60 cents payment. If there is anything whatever democratic about their intentions in this new party, the attitude should be "contract in". It is just a matter of mass intimidation when they bring this matter before the union membership for a vote and certain trade unions are affiliated with the congress. The situation is that an individual is obliged to declare himself against something. This is not the nature of the union men. They do not necessarily want to declare themselves against anything. Usually it is for something that they want to declare themselves. However, you have now put a question to the men throughout the unions in Canada, asking them to declare themselves against something. They do not wish to do this. The result is that through mass intimidation you have a great number of union men in this country being forced to pay into what is called the New Democratic party and I place the emphasis on the word "Democratic". If there were any guts whatsoever in the Canadian congress, the principle would be not to contract out but rather to contract in. That would be something in the way of a democratic movement. But that is not the situation. What you have is intimidation. You say the secret way of doing things is evil and dangerous. I say that intimidation is far worse than that.

I note that the hon. member said that it was an individual choice of every union across Canada. May I remind the hon. member now that what I am speaking of in the way of the democratic movement on the part of the New Democratic party are the rights of the individual, not the decision of the union bosses. This is a situation that I am fully aware of as it has gone on in my own union at home for some time, where the C.C.F. party collected a per capita tax from the united mine workers when the constitution of the mine workers itself did not permit it.

The hon. member speaks of the rights of individuals and refers to the choice of individual unions. But here was a case in which men were paying into the C.C.F. party or giving financial support to it while their moral support was going somewhere else. I put this question to the hon. member for Timmins and if I were permitted to do so I would put it in the way of a question to him and would allow him to answer it. They have the new party and they are going through this system of check-off whereby individual members will pay through a checkoff to a political fund. When the request is put to the various companies or businesses through which the check-off will be asked to be deducted, what will the position of the new party be if the individual who agrees to this check-off, agrees with the condition that the check-off be taken for a political fund, that it be taken off and directed to the Liberal party while another person's is directed to the Conservative party? Are they then going to stand up and ask for the privilege of a check-off for the three political parties?
As a member of the Conservative party I certainly do not want any part of a check-off from a union man who supports my party. If he supports me through my party he does it voluntarily. If he pays to my party, he does it voluntarily and secretly. This is going to be the last party that would stand up and consider doing or attempting to do what is being done by the New Democratic party, even without intimidation, namely to ask and to collect fees from people who will be forced to pay 60 cents towards a political fund while they will go out and support another party. Something that is evident right across this country. Although the C.C.F. for years have been collecting through the check-off from the workers of the country, they still have not been collecting the votes. We ourselves will depend on the secret way, on what the hon. member considers to be the dangerous and evil way. I say to him, however, that the dangerous and evil way is the intimidation which they are placing on the union men of this country by asking them not to contract in but to contract out.
As a union man himself, the hon. member is fully aware that this is the least democratic approach they could possibly put to any kind of fund or check-off from the men for any such purpose. As I said before, this is a situation that has gone on for years with the C.C.F. party in Cape Breton. A few of the locals stood up and cut it off. But for years they have been collecting that per capita tax from the members of the union down there while the union constitution itself denies this as a right.

The hon. member talks about the individual. Still and all, this was something that was jockied into position by the executive of the union at the time, whereby the men were not given a choice at all. This money was just taken from them and paid into the coffers of the C.C.F. party. I could go on and tell what happened to some of that money also.

Here is a condition being imposed upon the workers of this country by a per capita tax of 60 cents for every individual that belongs to a union affiliated with the Canadian labour congress. I say it is a shame. I would ask the hon. member, on union principles alone, to rise in his place and deny that contracting out is the proper way. It seems to me that in approaching this subject of campaign funds and campaign contributions the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) has fallen into a common error and has certainly departed from the direction and definition of his New Democratic party.
The tenor of the speech of the hon. member suggested that this matter of campaign giving was an evil thing; that the secrecy which clothed the contributions of individual members was hiding strange, dark shapes of men bent on twisting the purpose of parliament and corrupting the parties in this house.

When his colleague, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) was speaking to a similar bill in 1959 he used the word "subvert". He said:
These persons who contribute to political parties attempt to subvert parliament and the political parties within parliament.
I looked up the specific meaning of the word "subvert". It means, to overturn; to effect the destruction or overthrow of a party. The approach of the hon. member for Skeena and other hon. members who have taken this position in this discussion is repudiated by the people who have provided what has been described as the intellectual backdrop of the new party. The book "Social Purpose for Canada", edited by Michael Oliver, discusses many interesting things in connection with the new party. I have yet to appreciate how the principles defined in this book, which was written and rushed into print before the convention, are accepted by the New Democratic party.
I suggest that the hon. member read this book. I refer him particularly to page six and an article written by George Grant entitled "An Ethic of Community". He touches on this question of campaign giving and campaign contributions. He goes on to describe the support the established parties have obtained in various ways, and then he says this:
In saying all this, however, it is necessary to disclaim any "cops and robbers" or "conspiracy" view of history, which would imply that our society is at the mercy of a few wealthy and powerfbul men with Machiavellian intentions.
Perhaps the hon. member should have checked before he proceeded with this bill again.

the privilege of living in a democracy. I should explain that I have freely drawn during the course of my remarks from an article which appeared in the New York Times magazine in June 1958 when this campaign was initiated.
With the difficulties and failings of the experiment as I have outlined them, the campaign produced approximately $15 million. This was a non-presidential election.
