speechtext:
THE PREMIER Fredericton
July 19, 1961
My dear Prime Minister:-
It has now been possible for my colleagues and I to consider in detail your letter of June 16th regarding the federal-provincial tax-sharing arrangements to prevail after March 31, 1962. We are most disappointed that the federal government's position is rigidly unaltered from that outlined in your proposals at the conference in February. We do recognize that federal concessions have been made on two matters, but it is our firm belief that these are minor in nature and unrelated to the tax-sharing arrangements between our governments. It was also a further disappointment to us to learn that the federal government has seen fit to completely disregard all the proposals made by the provinces, both at the conference itself, and in the ensuing discussions by the committee of officials.
At the conference in February, our main criticism of the new proposals was directed at the provisions with respect to equalization payments generally, and the specific proposal to include the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants within the framework of these provisions. With respect to the equalization provisions, the new proposals remove emphasis from fiscal need, and substitute for it the increased ability to raise personal and corporate income taxes. This has the effect of discriminating against low income provinces like New Brunswick and will result in higher levels of taxation, relative to the rest of Canada, if national average standards of services are to be maintained.
The other aspect of the equalization provisions which we believe to be unrealistic and discriminatory, i.e., the inclusion of natural resource revenues in the formula, remains unchanged despite the many arguments which have been raised against it. In February, it was suggested that this proposal would provide a better measurement of the fiscal needs of the provinces, but we cannot see how this can possibly be the case. Surely, if better means of measurement are required, then a number of other provincial revenue sources must also be included. The
choice of this particular revenue source has neither been defended nor explained in this context, and your letter of June 16 merely repeats the federal sentiments expressed in February.
Generally, your proposals with respect to equalization payments will have the effect of reducing our revenues from this source by nearly two and one half million dollars. To offset this loss, it is proposed to increase the Atlantic provinces adjustment grant by three million dollars, which will provide a gain of some $600,000, or approximately one dollar per capita. This addition to revenues does not compare favourably with that of three dollars per capita for Ontario; $2.76 for Nova Scotia; $9.30 for Prince Edward Island; and $4.66 for Newfoundland. These are unalterable facts based on federal projections of revenues for the fiscal year 1962-63.
Furthermore, we strongly resent the inference drawn by the federal Minister of Finance in the House of Commons (see Hansard, July 11, 1961, p. 7928) that New Brunswick's share of the total of equalization payments available would rise substantially under the new proposals. The statement that New Brunswick's share of 6.4 per cent in 1957-58 would rise to 11.9 per cent under the new agreement is not only misleading but represents a rather insidious use of statistical techniques. A more proper comparison would be the last year of the current agreement with the first year of the new agreement. Excluding the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants, New Brunswick's share of the total equalization fund falls from 9.3 per cent to 8.8 per cent, while that for Nova Scotia rises from 10.8 per cent to 11.2 per cent; and that for Prince Edward Island, from 1.8 per cent to 1.9 per cent.
Finally, you have also indicated a complete rejection of our proposal that the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants should stand as a separate and distinct feature of the tax-sharing arrangements, and should not be included in the calculations of guaranteed payments to the provinces. This proposal was made in all sincerity based on the written record that these grants were of a special nature and were to be kept apart from the normal agreements. As such, my suggestion, which was reiterated by my officials at later

meetings, received the support of all the provinces of Canada, with the possible exception of one.
To all of us, it is clear that the Atlantic provinces will not get the full benefit of the ten million dollar increase proposed, but will in fact receive only a portion of it. We have consistently objected to this proposed procedure and have raised strong arguments against it. These arguments have not been answered, but have been dismissed with the comment that "this seems a reasonable procedure".
Both my colleagues and myself, along with the great majority of the other provinces, sincerely regret that the special nature and high objectives underlying these adjustment grants are to be destroyed merely to disguise the fact that the equalization formula provides a level of payments inconsistent with the fiscal needs of one entire region of Canada. I must urge you, Mr. Prime Minister, to reconsider whether the interests of the people of this region and the entire country are being best served by this procedure, which involves a saving to the federal treasury of only a few million dollars.
At the February conference, the federal proposals indicated that the provinces must assume the responsibility for levying their own personal and corporation income taxes to the extent of the federal withdrawal from these fields. Although we disagreed with this proposal, we did feel that this would provide the province with certain advantages in the field of provincial fiscal policy. In fact, you yourself suggested that the provinces would then be able "to impose, vary and adjust their levies from time to time as may be necessary in the light of their responsibilities to their provincial taxpayers and without recourse to the federal government".
From the subsequent meetings of officials and from your letter of June 16, we now find that the federal government wishes to restrict the provinces with respect to this type of flexibility in taxation. In other words, the province is not to be permitted the right of adjusting the tax base, or of altering the rate of progression, but has merely the right to determine the percentage of the federal rate which it is to impose.
In addition, there are no provisions to protect the interests of the provinces from the effects of changes in the federal rates which would significantly alter provincial revenues. The federal government, as indicated in your letter, reserves the right to alter its rates, whenever necessary for fiscal or other reasons, but the provincial percentage rates, once fixed, "must be constant throughout the year". These restrictions will inevitably produce a great deal of instability and uncertainty in
provincial financing, and may well result in significant reductions in revenues.
My reaction, and that of my colleagues, to these proposals is one of great disappointment and dissatisfaction. If there were available to us a suitable alternative, I am certain that our collective reaction would be a complete rejection of your proposals and a demand for more equitable treatment. However, no reasonable alternatives are available and we feel we must inevitably accept the federal position, no matter how arbitrarily it is taken. In view of this, and the many reasons expressed above, I am certain that many of the provincial premiers will join with me in urging you to call a final fiscal conference immediately, in order to permit further discussion of the proposals reiterated in your letter of June 16.
Having regard for the importance of the matter, and the fact that a precedent for such a conference exists, I am certain that you will agree that not to follow such a course would be a complete departure from the spirit of cooperation and flexibility which has been present in the past.
Yours very truly,

The Right Honourable John Diefenbaker Prime Minister of Canada Ottawa, Canada
Ottawa,
August 30th, 1961.
Honourable Louis J. Robichaud, M.L.A., Premier of New Brunswick,
Fredericton, New Brunswick.
My dear Premier,
Your letter of July 19 which requests a further dominion-provincial conference to consider the federal-provincial fiscal arrangements for the five year period commencing April 1st, 1962, has been given consideration.
It is a matter of regret that you have chosen to be so critical of the federal proposals which are in fact the most generous proposals ever offered by a government of Canada to the provinces. You have chosen to ignore the concessions and improvements contained in the proposals made at the dominion-provincial conference of February 23 and 24, and to refer only to what you describe as two minor concessions described in my letter of June 16. In this connection it is well to recall that the federal proposals advanced in my letter of June 16 followed three dominion-provincial conferences. At the conference of July 26 to 28, 1960, the provinces presented their views on the possible arrangements for the period after April 1, 1962. The

federal government considered these provincial proposals carefully which in the aggregate have been estimated to amount to over $2 billion per annum-an additional sum far in excess of what the federal government could or should impose on the taxpayers.
As a result of the consideration of the provincial proposals presented at the July conference, it became clear that the tax rental system was unsound and I made certain suggestions at the conference held October 26 and 27, 1960. I suggested that since the federal government was not in a position to finance the additional expenditure which the provinces judged to be necessary for the proper discharge of their responsibilities, the provinces themselves should again assume the task of levying their own taxes. I stated that the federal government was prepared to recommend to parliament that the federal taxes on personal income, corporation income, and estates be reduced by 14-9-50, that is, by the standard rates then in effect. In addition, the government was prepared to recommend that an equalization fund of $220 million per annum be made available to the provinces to be divided as they saw fit provided that the Atlantic provinces each received at least as much under agreed division as they then received from equalization, Atlantic provinces adjustment grants, and the additional grant to Newfoundland.
Apart from the fact that some provinces were not anxious to reassume their constitutional responsibility for levying taxes for the support of their expenditures, provincial criticism of the October suggestions was largely on the grounds that the federal withdrawal should be greater than existing standard rates and that equalization should include a growth factor. The federal government responded to these provincial requests by making very generous concessions in the proposals of February 23 and 24, 1961. The federal withdrawal of 14-9-50 offered at the October conference was increased to 16-9-50 for the first years of the new period and was to rise progressively throughout the period, reaching 20-9-50 in the final year. This was an increase of more than 40 per cent in the federal withdrawal from personal income tax over the present share and over the withdrawal offered at the October conference, and it raised the provincial share of personal income tax to an amount in the final year of double the 10 per cent in effect when this government took office. Second, the federal government proposed a new system of equalization broadened to take account of the most variable of all provincial revenues, namely, revenues from natural resources. However, equalization payments under the system proposed will rise year by year with the growth in standard taxes and revenue from natural resources thus fully meeting the request of the provinces for the inclusion of a growth factor. Third, the federal government offered to recommend to parliament an increase of $10 million per annum in the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants. Fourth, the federal government offered to collect without charge the provincial personal income and corporation income taxes at whatever levels of tax the provinces chose to impose thus restoring to them without adding to their administrative costs a freedom and flexibility they had been so long denied under the tax rental system.
The February proposals constituted considerable additions to and changes of the October suggestions and represented the federal government's willingness and desire to achieve an equitable and harmonious settlement with the provinces within the framework of the constitution. Following the February conference, careful consideration was given to further representations of the provincial premiers. This was done both at the official level in two meetings of the continuing committee on fiscal and economic matters and by further review of the various aspects of the proposals by the federal government itself. As was explained in my letter of June 16, the government took account of the representations which had been made with respect to the sharing of the tax on certain public utility corporations and agreed to extend this sharing for the next five years. In addition, the government offered a substantial concession with respect to taxes on logging income by offering to provide a tax credit if the provinces would take similar action although bearing a smaller part of the cost.
You have disregarded these latter concessions and the considerable adjustments which were made to the original October suggestions for the benefit of the provinces. I am reminded of the aptness of a statement made by the then prime minister, the Right Honourable Louis St. Laurent, as shown on page 2016 of Hansard of March 12, 1956. In answer to a question as to whether any further concessions were made to the provinces, he replied, "Mr. Speaker, the provinces would not admit that anything that is proposed is a concession".
Your letter raises a number of points which you allege support your request for another dominion-provincial conference. These have already received careful consideration. In my letter of June 16 I dealt at length with the issues raised and the decisions which have been reached with respect to the various aspects of the proposals. The Minister of Finance, in introducing the new federal-pro-

vincial fiscal arrangements bill in the House of Commons on July 11, 1961, gave a complete statement of the federal proposals and I note from your letter that you have read this statement. Despite the fact that we have given a full explanation of the federal proposals, I shall now attempt to clarify certain points to which you allude.
You refer at a number of points in your letter to the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants and contend that these grants should be kept separate from the other fiscal arrangements. In fact, the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants will continue to be a separate grant and the increase of $10 million in the total amount will benefit your province to the extent of $3 million per annum, which is the 30 per cent share of the additional grant of $10 million. This grant will be paid separately and is in no way connected with the basic equalization formula which ensures that New Brunswick will receive an equalization payment sufficient to raise revenues from the standard taxes and 50 per cent of the natural resource revenues to the per capita national average yield. This fact is clear from the provisions of Bill C-122 which was introduced into the House of Commons on July 12, 1961. In addition to providing for a basic equalization formula based on the standard taxes plus 50 per cent of natural resource revenue and the separate Atlantic provinces adjustment grants, increased in total by $10 million, the government has embodied in the bill two guarantee provisions which will lead in certain cases to the payment of even higher amounts of equalization. Under these provisions, no province will receive less than it received in the preceding year and no province which is below the national average in the yield of standard taxes and 50 per cent of natural resources revenue will receive less than enough to bring its total return to the amount it would have received under the preceding arrangements. It is in these guarantee provisions only that it was thought reasonable to take account of the increase in the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants in the same way as we would take account of all other payments under the previous arrangements. These guarantees ensured that no province below the national average could be worse off under the new arrangements than under the old arrangements. I should point out to you that this is on the basis of a personal income tax rate of 16 per cent Provision is made for the rate to rise to 20 per cent. If the 20 per cent rate were used instead of the 16 per cent rate, you would find that the over-all gain to New Brunswick would be in excess of $3 million per annum.
You have alleged that the new proposals remove emphasis from fiscal need and substitute for it increased ability to raise personal and corporate income taxes. Nothing could be farther removed from the facts. By instituting the system of Atlantic provinces adjustment grants and by increasing them for the coming period by a further $10 million per annum, by continuing the special payment of $8 million per annum to the province of Newfoundland, and by providing a new equalization formula based on the national average and including 50 per cent of the most variable of all provincial revenues, namely, natural resources, this government has ensured that a large percentage of fiscal aid payments will go to the less well to do provinces. This fact is well illustrated by the comparisons made by the Minister of Finance in the House of Commons on July 11, 1961, and to which you refer on page 2 of your letter. While the proposals have increased the emphasis on fiscal need, they also permit the provinces to cultivate their tax fields in the way each province deems fit. There is nothing inconsistent in these objectives. I must reaffirm this government's attention to the fiscal problems of the less well to do regions of Canada and repeat that its performance in this regard goes far beyond anything that has ever been done in the past.
I find it difficult to understand your opposition to the inclusion of 50 per cent of natural resources revenue in the equalization formula. As already stated, the natural resource factor was included because variations from province to province in per capita natural resource revenue are far more extreme than variations in any other provincial revenues. Indeed, the inclusion of the natural resource factor directly benefits the province of New Brunswick where the per capita revenue from natural resources is below the national average.
You refer also to the conditions under which the federal government will collect provincial taxes free of charge and cite these as evidence of a lack of flexibility in the federal proposals. The federal government's answer is that it is endeavouring to give the provinces all the freedom that is possible, subject only to the limitations of administrative feasilibity and our concern for the convenience of taxpayers.
It is the earnest desire of the federal government to achieve harmonious and equitable fiscal arrangements with the provinces. In a co-operative spirit we have sought a more equal and equitable partnership with the provinces. I hope that upon reconsideration the financial benefits of the new arrangements and the greater freedom and flexilibity which they afford to your province will commend themselves to you.
Yours sincerely,
John G. Diefenbaker.
Monday, September 18, 1961
